If every file you own direct-plays without conversion, the Synology DS923+ will happily serve more simultaneous 4K streams than either of them, because it never has to touch its CPU. The one fact to settle before you compare anything else: hardware transcoding needs an Intel integrated GPU and a paid Plex Pass — an AMD-based NAS cannot do it at all, no matter how fast its processor is.

 Best overall: TerraMaster F4-424 Pro
 The F4-424 Pro is the pick when transcoding is the job. Per TerraMaster’s spec sheet, its Core i3-N305 pairs a 32-execution-unit Intel UHD iGPU with 8 GB of DDR5 that expands to 32 GB — more headroom than the Celeron-class boxes it undercuts on price. In practice that translates to roughly four to five simultaneous 4K-to-1080p transcodes, and about half that if Plex is tone-mapping HDR to SDR at the same time.
 Who it suits: households with a mix of clients — an Apple TV 4K, a couple of phones, a browser tab — where somebody is always forcing a conversion. Main trade-off: TerraMaster’s TOS software is less polished than Synology’s DSM or QNAP’s QTS, and the third-party app catalog is thinner. You are buying silicon, not software.
 Best value four-bay: QNAP TS-464
 The TS-464 uses a Celeron N5095 with a 16-EU iGPU, 8 GB of DDR4 (16 GB max), dual 2.5GbE ports and two M.2 NVMe slots for cache or a separate metadata volume. It handles two to three 4K transcodes comfortably and will direct-play everything you throw at it. QTS is a mature platform with a proper container station, which matters if you want to run Plex alongside the *arr stack.
 Who it suits: the buyer who wants a proven four-bay chassis and doesn’t want to learn a new operating system. Main trade-off: roughly half the transcoding throughput of the N305 for only about $50–$100 less, and QNAP’s firmware cadence means occasional update babysitting.
 Best small starter box: Synology DS224+
 The DS224+ is the cheapest route into genuine Quick Sync transcoding. Its Celeron J4125 and 12-EU iGPU will push one, occasionally two, 4K-to-1080p conversions, and DSM remains the easiest NAS operating system to live with. The catch is the 2 GB of soldered RAM — plan on adding a stick to reach the 6 GB ceiling, because Plex’s metadata and thumbnail database is memory-hungry.
 Who it suits: a first NAS for one or two viewers, or a secondary box for a bedroom. Main trade-off: two bays means RAID 1 gives you only one drive’s worth of usable capacity, and there is no upgrade path except replacing the whole unit.
 Best for large 4K libraries: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus is the only pick here with 10GbE built in, and its Pentium Gold 8505 carries a 48-EU iGPU — the strongest transcode engine in this group, good for five to six simultaneous 4K-to-1080p conversions. DDR5 expands to 64 GB, which is overkill for Plex but welcome if you also run virtual machines. The 10GbE port matters more than it sounds: a 4K remux peaks around 80–100 Mbps, so a 1GbE link saturates at roughly nine direct streams before overhead, while 10GbE removes the network as a bottleneck entirely.
 Who it suits: anyone with a 20 TB-plus remux collection and a wired 10GbE switch or a direct-attach workstation. Main trade-off: UGOS is the youngest operating system in this roundup, and the ecosystem is still catching up on polish.
 Best for direct-play purists: Synology DS923+
 Per Synology’s spec sheet, the DS923+’s AMD Ryzen R1600 has no integrated graphics — which means no Quick Sync, which means every conversion falls to two cores of CPU. Software-transcoding 4K HEVC on that chip is not realistic; it will stutter. But if your clients all direct-play, the DS923+ is arguably the best pure file server here: ECC memory support, a PCIe slot for a 10GbE card, and DSM’s mature storage management.
 Who it suits: a library encoded in formats your players already understand, or a household that keeps a separate mini-PC as the Plex server and uses the NAS purely for storage. Main trade-off: buy it expecting to transcode and you will be disappointed.
 How to choose: the numbers that actually matter
 1. Confirm you need transcoding at all
 Direct play uses no CPU — the NAS just streams bytes. Transcoding happens when the client can’t handle the file’s codec, container, resolution or subtitle format, or when remote viewers are capped by upload bandwidth. Check your library and your players first; if everything direct-plays, you can spend the transcoding budget on drive bays instead.
 2. Budget for Plex Pass, because hardware transcoding is locked behind it
 Plex’s documentation is explicit: GPU-accelerated transcoding is a Plex Pass feature. Without it, the iGPU sits idle and Plex falls back to software encoding. A lifetime pass costs roughly the same as one extra drive, and it is the single highest-value purchase in this entire build.
 3. Count bays by capacity, not by ambition
 A 4-bay chassis in RAID 5 or Synology’s SHR gives you three drives of usable space plus one for parity. A 2-bay in RAID 1 gives you one. If your library is 15 TB and growing, two bays means buying two 20 TB drives to store 20 TB — four bays means four 8 TB drives to store 24 TB, usually for less money.
 4. Match the network port to your peak bitrate
 Add up the peak bitrate of your busiest simultaneous streams and leave 30% headroom. Three 4K remuxes at 90 Mbps is 270 Mbps, which 1GbE handles fine. Ten of them is 900 Mbps, which it does not — that is when 2.5GbE or 10GbE stops being a luxury.
 Worked example: sizing a 4-bay NAS for a 400-film 4K library
 Assume 400 UHD remuxes at an average of 60 GB each. That is 24,000 GB, or about 24 TB of media. Add Plex metadata: artwork and database files run a few gigabytes, but generated video thumbnails can consume 100 GB or more on a large library, so budget 25 TB total.
 Four 12 TB NAS drives in RAID 5 give 36 TB raw usable, minus roughly 10% for filesystem overhead, landing near 32 TB. That leaves about 7 TB of growth room. At typical 2026 pricing of $15–$20 per terabyte for NAS-rated CMR drives, the storage costs $720–$960, on top of a $450–$650 chassis — call it $1,200–$1,600 all in, or roughly $3–$4 per film stored.
 Now the transcoding side: a 16-EU Celeron iGPU handles two to three 4K-to-1080p conversions; a 32-EU i3-N305 handles four to five; a 48-EU Pentium Gold handles five to six. Enable HDR tone mapping and cut every one of those numbers roughly in half, because tone mapping is a second GPU pass on the same silicon.

 Ownership realities: what wears out and what trips people up
 Drives fail first. NAS-rated CMR disks are typically rated around one million hours MTBF, which in a four-drive array usually means one failure somewhere in years three to five. Buy drives from different batches and keep a cold spare on the shelf.
 Avoid SMR drives. Shingled magnetic recording drives stall badly during RAID rebuilds. Check the spec sheet for “CMR” before you buy — this is the most common costly mistake in budget NAS builds.
 SSD cache is not a transcoding upgrade. It accelerates metadata and random I/O, not GPU work. If you have two M.2 slots, one cache drive plus one dedicated volume for Plex metadata is a better split than two mirrored cache drives.
 RAID is not a backup. It survives a dead disk; it does not survive an accidental delete, ransomware, or a power surge. Follow 3-2-1: three copies, two media types, one off-site.
 Heat and dust are the slow killers. Keep ambient temperature under 30°C, clean the intake filters every three to six months, and expect fans to be the first non-drive component to need replacing.
 Wire it. Wi-Fi adds jitter and typically halves usable throughput; a NAS on wireless will stutter on high-bitrate 4K even when the CPU is idle.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can I run Plex on a NAS without an Intel CPU?
 Yes, but only with software transcoding. AMD-based units like the Synology DS923+ handle direct play perfectly well and can serve several 4K streams at once, since streaming without conversion costs almost no CPU. The moment a client forces a 4K HEVC conversion, however, a low-power AMD chip will not keep up and playback will buffer.
 Do I really need a Plex Pass for hardware transcoding?
 Yes. Plex’s documentation lists GPU-accelerated transcoding as a Plex Pass feature, so without a subscription the integrated GPU stays idle and everything falls back to CPU encoding. This is why two NAS units with identical processors can perform completely differently — the difference is the license, not the hardware.
 How many simultaneous 4K streams can a NAS handle?
 Direct play is limited by disk and network, not CPU: on 1GbE expect roughly five to nine concurrent 4K remux streams before the link saturates. Hardware transcoding is limited by the iGPU: two to three streams on a 16-EU Celeron, four to five on a 32-EU Core i3-N305, and five to six on a 48-EU Pentium Gold. Enabling HDR tone mapping roughly halves each figure.
 Is RAID enough to protect my media library?
 No. RAID protects against a single drive failure by keeping the array running; it does nothing about deletion, corruption, theft or fire, because every change is mirrored instantly to the parity drive. Treat RAID as uptime insurance and keep a separate backup — for a large remux library, an external drive rotation or a second NAS at another address is the practical approach.
 How much RAM does a Plex NAS actually need?
 Plex itself is light, but the metadata database and thumbnail generation are not. Four gigabytes is a reasonable floor for a library of a few hundred titles; eight gigabytes is comfortable; more than sixteen only pays off if you also run virtual machines or containers. On the Synology DS224+, the 2 GB stock configuration is genuinely tight — upgrading to 6 GB is the first thing to do.
 Should I buy a 2-bay or a 4-bay NAS for Plex?
 Buy four bays unless space or budget is genuinely tight. A 2-bay array in RAID 1 wastes half your raw capacity on mirroring, so storing 20 TB requires two 20 TB drives — often more expensive than four 8 TB drives in RAID 5, which would give you 24 TB usable. Four bays also let you expand one drive at a time instead of replacing the whole unit.

 The enclosure is half the bill
Every NAS here ships empty. NAS-rated CMR drives (WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf) are bought
 separately and priced per drive by capacity, so the real budget is enclosure plus two or more
 drives. Size the drives for the data you will have in three years, not the data you have today.
 2-bay mirror math, or 4-bay (n-1) math
A 2-bay in RAID 1 gives you ONE drive's worth of usable space: 2×8TB = 8TB. A 4-bay in RAID 5 or
 single-redundancy SHR gives up only one drive: 4×8TB ≈ 24TB usable, with one-at-a-time upgrades
 instead of the 2-bay's both-drives upgrade trap. At this bracket the F4-424 is the 4-bay that fits.
 How many bays do you really need? → 
 Hardware value or software polish, not both
Synology sells software polish on older, slower hardware (a 2020-era Celeron, 2GB base RAM, no NVMe
 on the DS225+). QNAP, TerraMaster and UGREEN sell current hardware (2.5GbE, NVMe, 8GB) with software that
 is either busier (QTS), less mature (TOS) or younger (UGOS Pro). Decide which you are paying for.
 The spec that splits this bracket: 2.5GbE vs 1GbE
 2.5GbE matters because 1GbE is the real bottleneck in most NAS setups. A 1GbE link tops out around 110–118MB/s of actual throughput — and a single modern hard drive already reads at roughly 180–280MB/s sequentially, so on gigabit you're leaving half the drive's speed on the table, and a RAID array or NVMe cache is throttled even harder. 2.5GbE lifts the ceiling to ~280MB/s, roughly matching one fast HDD and dramatically improving large-file transfers. It's the single most worthwhile 'speed' upgrade for home NAS; 10GbE only pays off with NVMe pools or many-drive arrays. All four picks now ship 2.5GbE: the TS-264 and F4-424 with two ports, the
 DXP2800 and the Synology DS225+ with one (the DS225+ pairs it with a 1GbE port; its predecessor, the
 DS224+, was 1GbE only).
 2.5GbE vs 1GbE, in full → 
 How do the four compare on the specs that decide it?
From our master spec data: CPU class, RAM ceiling, networking, NVMe, operating system and whether the
 chip can hardware-transcode. None of these four has ECC; that is a feature of the prosumer tier below.

 What you give up versus the tier above
Just above this bracket, the Synology DS425+ buys DSM at four bays: the same J4125

 DS925+ , is what more money buys: ECC memory expandable to 32GB and two 2.5GbE ports, but
 no integrated GPU, so it is a poor Plex transcoding box, which is exactly the job many budget buyers want

 Which drives belong in a budget NAS?
 NAS-rated drives use CMR (conventional magnetic recording); many cheap desktop and external drives use SMR (shingled), which overlaps tracks to pack in more capacity but must rewrite whole zones on write, making sustained and random writes slow. In a NAS this matters most during a RAID rebuild: an SMR drive can slow a rebuild to a crawl or cause it to drop out of the array, risking a second failure before it finishes. Use CMR NAS drives (WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf) in an array; the plain WD Red was infamously SMR. Always confirm CMR on the spec sheet. The temptation at this bracket is to save on drives after spending on the
 enclosure. Do not: a rebuild after a failure is your single window of vulnerability, and an SMR drive
 stretching that window is exactly the risk you bought RAID to avoid.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best NAS under $500? ▼ For most buyers it is the QNAP TS-264: a 2-bay with dual 2.5GbE, two M.2 NVMe slots and 8GB of RAM out of the box, which is more hardware than any rival at its tier. If you want four bays in the same money, the TerraMaster F4-424 is the raw hardware-value pick (Intel N95, 8GB DDR5 expandable to 32GB, dual 2.5GbE) and openly supports TrueNAS or Unraid. If you want the most polished software and the least tinkering, the Synology DS225+ is the turnkey box, at the cost of 2GB base RAM (6GB maximum), one 2.5GbE port and no NVMe. All of these are enclosure prices only: the drives are a separate purchase, and prices move, so confirm the bracket on the live listing.
 Does 'under $500' include the drives? ▼ No. Every NAS on this page ships as an empty enclosure, and the drives are the other half of the purchase, priced per drive by capacity. Budget for NAS-rated CMR drives (WD Red Plus or Seagate IronWolf) on top of the enclosure. Avoid SMR (shingled) drives in a RAID array: their slow rewrite behavior can make a rebuild crawl or fail, and the plain WD Red (non-Plus) and many cheap desktop or shucked drives are SMR. Confirm CMR on the spec sheet.
 2-bay or 4-bay at this budget? ▼ A 2-bay mirror (RAID 1) gives you one drive's worth of usable space (2×8TB = 8TB) and covers most homes: photos, documents, PC backups and a light media library. A 4-bay in RAID 5 or single-redundancy SHR gives you roughly (n-1) drives of usable space (4×8TB ≈ 24TB) plus one-at-a-time capacity upgrades and an escape hatch to two-drive redundancy. At this bracket the TerraMaster F4-424 is the 4-bay that fits; a 4-bay running only two drives at first is often the smarter buy because it keeps a growth path a 2-bay can never offer.
 Which budget NAS is best for Plex or Jellyfin? ▼ All four picks have Intel CPUs with integrated graphics that handle hardware transcoding: the QNAP TS-264 (N5105), TerraMaster F4-424 (N95), UGREEN DXP2800 (N100) and Synology DS225+ (J4125, H.264/H.265). The TS-264, F4-424 and DXP2800 have the edge for a media-heavy setup because of newer CPUs, more RAM and NVMe slots; the DS225+'s 2GB base RAM (6GB maximum) makes it the weakest of the four for that job.
 Is the Synology DS225+ worth it over the cheaper-hardware brands? ▼ It is if the appliance experience is what you are buying. DSM is the most polished, best-documented NAS operating system, with the widest first-party app ecosystem, and the DS225+ is the lowest-friction way into NAS. What you give up is hardware: a 2020-era Celeron J4125, 2GB base RAM (6GB maximum), one 2.5GbE port rather than two, and no NVMe. QNAP, TerraMaster and UGREEN sell current hardware (2.5GbE, NVMe, 8GB) with software that is either busier (QTS), less mature (TOS) or younger (UGOS Pro).
 Is RAID on a budget NAS a backup? ▼ No. RAID (except RAID 0) protects against one drive failing, keeping the array online while you replace the disk. It does nothing against accidental deletion, ransomware, corruption, theft, fire or a power surge, all of which hit the live array and every mirror at once. Treat the NAS as one copy in a 3-2-1 scheme: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 off-site. A budget NAS plus a cloud or off-site copy is a real setup; a NAS alone is not.

We're a research-based site: we analyze manufacturer specifications, storage and filesystem engineering,

Best NAS for Plex in 2026: Synology vs UGREEN — Honest Buyer’s Guide | Self Host Life Skip to content ⚡ Quick Answer
 For most users in 2026, the best NAS for Plex is the Synology DS224+ (~$300). It has Intel Quick Sync hardware transcoding, proven Plex compatibility, and the polished DSM software. UGREEN DXP2800 (~$297) is the strongest alternative with newer hardware.
 ⚠️ Important: skip the 2025 Synology DS225+ — it lost hardware transcoding.
 💰 Budget · Synology DS223j · ~$170 — Direct-play streaming only, no transcoding. Fine if all your devices support native playback.
 ⭐ Best Overall · Synology DS224+ · ~$300 — Intel Quick Sync transcoding, DSM software, proven for Plex. Recommended for most users.
 🚀 Best Value · UGREEN DXP2800 · ~$297 — Intel N100, 8GB DDR5, 2.5GbE — newer hardware at the same price. Software still maturing.
 ⚡ Power User · UGREEN DXP4800 Plus · ~$600 — Intel Pentium Gold, 10GbE, 4 bays. Handles 10+ simultaneous streams.
 Why Picking the Right NAS for Plex Matters in 2026
 A NAS (Network Attached Storage) running Plex turns your media library into Netflix — accessible from your TV, phone, or laptop anywhere in the world. The wrong NAS makes streaming a slideshow of stutters. The right one just works.
 The Plex-specific requirement most buyers overlook: hardware transcoding. If your TV speaks one video format and your file is in another, the NAS has to convert it on the fly. Without dedicated transcoding hardware, even a 4-core CPU struggles.
 Based on community testing in r/PleX and benchmark comparisons, three NAS models consistently top the recommendations: Synology DS224+, UGREEN DXP2800, and (for power users) UGREEN DXP4800 Plus.
 ⚠️ Important 2025 update: Synology’s newer DS225+ model uses the same J4125 CPU as the DS224+ but Synology removed the kernel graphics driver, disabling Plex hardware transcoding. The older DS224+ is actually the better Plex pick. We’ll explain why below.
 The Hardware Transcoding Factor (Critical for Plex)
 Before comparing models, you need to understand transcoding. It’s the single biggest factor that separates ‘best NAS for Plex’ from ‘NAS that happens to run Plex.’
 Direct Play vs Transcoding
 Direct Play: The NAS sends the file as-is. Your device plays it. Almost no CPU needed. Works when device and file format match.
 Transcoding: The NAS converts the file to a format your device understands. Needs CPU power. Without hardware acceleration (Intel Quick Sync), transcoding 4K kills the NAS.
 In practice: smart TVs, modern phones, and Apple TVs handle most files directly. Older devices, web browsers, and remote streaming over slow connections trigger transcoding.
 Why Intel CPUs Beat AMD for Plex NAS
 Intel Celeron and N100 CPUs include Quick Sync — a built-in video accelerator. AMD’s Ryzen R1600 (in Synology DS923+) does not. For Plex specifically, Intel beats AMD.
 That’s why the older DS224+ outperforms the newer DS225+ for Plex. It’s also why UGREEN’s Intel N100 in the DXP2800 outperforms Synology’s Ryzen options.
 Synology DS224+ — Best NAS for Plex Overall
 The DS224+ is the de facto standard for entry-level Plex NAS in 2026. It’s been the top recommendation in self-hosting communities for two years for good reason: it just works .
 DS224+ Specs
 CPU: Intel Celeron J4125 (quad-core, 2.0GHz, Quick Sync)
 RAM: 2GB DDR4 (upgradeable to 6GB)
 Bays: 2 (up to 36TB)
 Network: 2x Gigabit Ethernet
 Plex transcoding: Yes (H.264 and HEVC)
 Power: ~25W idle
 Price: ~$300 diskless
 Why It Wins for Plex
 Hardware transcoding works. The J4125’s Intel Graphics 600 chip handles 2-3 simultaneous 4K transcodes without breaking a sweat. For a typical 1-2 user household, this is plenty.
 DSM software is polished. Synology’s DiskStation Manager is the most refined NAS OS on the market. Plex installs in two clicks via the Package Center. Beginners can set this up in under an hour.
 Proven reliability. Two years of community testing. Thousands of self-hosters run DS224+ as their daily Plex server. The forums have answers to every conceivable problem.
 DS224+ Drawbacks (Honest)
 Only 1GbE network: Most users won’t notice, but if you have 2.5GbE devices, you’re capped.
 2GB RAM is tight: Spend $30 on a 4GB SO-DIMM upgrade. Total cost still under $340.
 Only 2 bays: Max ~36TB. If you need more, look at the DS923+ or DXP4800 Plus.
 Older hardware: J4125 is from 2019. Still capable for Plex, but feels dated next to the N100.
 Check DS224+ Price on Amazon → 
 UGREEN DXP2800 — Best Value Alternative
 UGREEN entered the NAS market in 2024 and immediately disrupted it. The DXP2800 offers noticeably newer hardware than the DS224+ at the same price . The catch: UGREEN’s software (UGOS) is younger and less polished than Synology’s DSM.
 DXP2800 Specs
 CPU: Intel N100 (quad-core, Alder Lake-N, Quick Sync)
 RAM: 8GB DDR5 (upgradeable to 16GB+)
 Bays: 2 (plus 2 M.2 NVMe slots)
 Network: 2.5GbE
 Plex transcoding: Yes (H.264, HEVC, including AV1 decode)
 Power: ~10W idle
 Price: ~$297 diskless on Amazon
 Why It’s the Best Value
 Modern Intel N100 CPU. Released in 2023, the N100 outperforms the J4125 in every benchmark while using less power. Plex transcoding is faster and quieter.
 8GB RAM standard. The DS224+ ships with 2GB. The DXP2800 ships with 8GB DDR5. That’s a meaningful difference for running Plex alongside Docker containers.
 2.5GbE built-in. Faster network transfers if your router supports it. The DS224+ caps at 1GbE.
 DXP2800 Drawbacks (Honest)
 Software still maturing: UGOS works, but lacks the app ecosystem and polish of Synology DSM.
 Smaller community: Fewer tutorials, fewer Reddit answers. You’ll occasionally hit edge cases without easy fixes.
 Younger brand: UGREEN’s track record in NAS is 2 years. Synology’s is 25+. Hardware seems solid, but long-term reliability is unknown.

 For most readers asking ‘best NAS for Plex’ in 2026, the DS224+ is the safer choice . The DXP2800 is the smart choice.
 Budget Pick — Synology DS223j (Under $200)
 If your budget is tight and your devices support direct play, the Synology DS223j at ~$170 is the cheapest legitimate Plex NAS in 2026.
 DS223j Honest Take
 Realtek RTD1619B ARM CPU. No Quick Sync. Direct play only — no transcoding.
 2GB RAM (not upgradeable). Enough for Plex + 1-2 light services.
 2 bays. Same expansion as DS224+.
 DSM software. Same polished software experience.
 Only buy this if: All your devices natively support your file formats. Modern smart TVs, Apple TVs, NVIDIA Shield, and current-gen phones usually do. Older devices, browsers, and remote streaming will fail.
 If in doubt, spend the extra $100 on the DS224+. The hardware transcoding is worth it for the next 5+ years of unknown future devices.
 Power User Pick — UGREEN DXP4800 Plus
 For libraries over 10TB or households streaming to 5+ devices simultaneously, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus at ~$600 is the value champion in the 4-bay segment.
 DXP4800 Plus Specs
 CPU: Intel Pentium Gold 8505 (5-core, hybrid architecture)
 RAM: 8GB DDR5 (upgradeable)
 Bays: 4 (plus 2 M.2 NVMe)
 Network: 1x 10GbE + 1x 2.5GbE
 Concurrent Plex streams: 10+ simultaneous
 The Pentium Gold 8505 is dramatically more powerful than the N100 — closer to a desktop CPU. Combined with 10GbE networking, this NAS handles serious media server duties. Synology has no equivalent at this price point . The DS923+ ($600) lacks Intel Quick Sync.
 Check Synology DS923+ (Plex Power Alternative) → 
 NAS Models to Avoid for Plex in 2026
 Avoid: Synology DS225+ (2025 release)
 Despite being newer, the DS225+ is worse for Plex than the older DS224+ . Synology silently removed the kernel graphics driver, disabling Plex hardware transcoding for H.264 and HEVC. Same CPU (J4125), same form factor, same price — but no transcoding.
 This was a deliberate decision Synology confirmed in support tickets. Workarounds exist (unofficial SSH methods), but most buyers shouldn’t have to hack their brand-new NAS.
 Avoid: Synology DS923+ for Plex Specifically
 The DS923+ is a great NAS — just not for Plex transcoding. Its AMD Ryzen R1600 CPU lacks Intel Quick Sync. For non-Plex workloads (general storage, Docker, file serving), it’s excellent. For Plex with transcoding, pick the DS224+ or UGREEN DXP4800 Plus instead.
 Avoid: Cheap ‘no-name’ NAS units under $150
 Brands like Buffalo LinkStation, generic Chinese NAS units, and dust-collecting older models from 2019 fail at Plex in 2026. Their CPUs can’t handle modern codecs, their software lacks Plex integration, and their RAM is often non-upgradeable. False economy.
 Which Hard Drives Should You Pair with Your Plex NAS?
 ⚠️ HDD prices in 2026: Hard drive prices jumped about 46% since September 2025 due to AI infrastructure demand. A 4TB NAS drive that was $80 in mid-2025 now costs $115+. Factor this into your budget.
 For Plex NAS use, you want CMR (not SMR) NAS-rated drives. Three brands dominate:
 WD Red Plus: Most popular. $115-130 for 4TB, $200-240 for 8TB.
 Seagate IronWolf: Slightly faster, similar price.
 Toshiba N300: Cheapest option, slightly louder.
 Recommended size: Start with 2x 4TB in RAID 1 (4TB usable). For media libraries over 2TB, go 2x 8TB. Avoid drives under 4TB — the price per terabyte is poor.
 Important: the 2025 Synology drive lock-in issue (where new Plus models required Synology-branded drives) was reversed in DSM 7.3 (October 2025). Third-party drives now work normally on all 2025 and 2026 Plus models. Make sure your DSM is updated.
 Beyond the NAS — What Else You Need for Plex
 Budget for these too:
 Hard drives: Not included with NAS. $230-460 for 2-4 drives.
 Plex Pass (optional): $6.99/mo, $69.99/yr, $249.99 for five years, or $749.99 lifetime (plex.tv, checked August 2026). Required for hardware transcoding. Worth it if you have non-Plex devices — see Jellyfin vs Plex for whether it is worth paying at all, and the Jellyfin setup guide if you decide it is not.
 UPS (uninterruptible power supply): $50-100. Protects against power surges and gives clean shutdown during outages.
 RAM upgrade for DS224+: $30 for a 4GB SO-DIMM. Recommended.
 Total realistic cost for a working setup: $550-700 for a 2-bay NAS with 8TB drives. Compare to $25-50/month for streaming subscriptions — you break even in 12-18 months.
 Frequently Asked Questions About the Best NAS for Plex
 Is Synology DS224+ still the best NAS for Plex in 2026?
 Yes, for most users. Despite being released in 2024, the DS224+ outperforms the newer DS225+ for Plex specifically (since Synology removed hardware transcoding from the DS225+). The combination of Intel Quick Sync, polished DSM software, and proven reliability still makes it the safest pick.
 Does the new Synology DS225+ work for Plex?
 Yes, but with reduced functionality. The DS225+ uses the same Intel J4125 CPU as the DS224+ but Synology disabled the kernel graphics driver, removing hardware transcoding. Direct play works fine. Transcoding falls back to slow software-only mode. The older DS224+ is the better Plex pick.
 Is UGREEN reliable enough for a NAS purchase?
 Probably. UGREEN has been making electronics for 13+ years and entered NAS in 2024. Their DXP series has positive reviews and a 2-year warranty. The unknown is long-term software updates — Synology’s 10-year support track record doesn’t yet exist for UGREEN.
 How much RAM do I need for a Plex NAS?
 4GB minimum for a single Plex server, 8GB if you’re running additional services like Sonarr or Radarr. The DXP2800 ships with 8GB. The DS224+ ships with 2GB but upgrades easily to 6GB for $30. Most Plex performance issues blamed on CPU are actually RAM-bound.
 Can I run Plex from Korea with these NAS?
 Yes. Plex works globally — the NAS sits at your home/office, and Plex clients connect via the internet. For Korean users, all three picks above (DS224+, DXP2800, DXP4800 Plus) are available on Amazon Korea or via direct import. Synology has stronger local support in Korea.
 What’s the difference between Plex and Jellyfin on NAS?
 Plex is more polished, requires a free account, and offers Plex Pass paid features. Jellyfin is fully free, fully self-hosted, with no external account. Most NAS units run both equally well — Plex has slightly better hardware transcoding support on Synology DSM.
 Should I build my own NAS instead of buying one?
 Only if you enjoy Linux administration. A DIY NAS with TrueNAS or Unraid costs $300-500 and gives more flexibility, but requires significantly more setup time. For most users, a pre-built Synology or UGREEN saves 10+ hours of configuration.
 The Bottom Line — Best NAS for Plex in 2026
 💡 Final Pick: For most Plex users in 2026, the Synology DS224+ remains the best NAS — proven reliability, Intel Quick Sync transcoding, polished DSM software, huge community. The UGREEN DXP2800 is the smarter pick for users who want newer hardware and don’t mind UGOS’s learning curve.
 Avoid the Synology DS225+ despite its ‘newer’ label — it lost hardware transcoding. Avoid the Synology DS923+ for Plex specifically — its AMD CPU lacks Quick Sync.
 Budget under $200? Synology DS223j if your devices support direct play. Need 4 bays and 10GbE? UGREEN DXP4800 Plus . Everything else is in between.
 Once your NAS is set up, you’ll want a reliable way to access it remotely. See my guide on self-hosting on a $5 VPS for a cheap reverse-proxy setup that works perfectly with Synology and UGREEN NAS.

 For most homes running Jellyfin or Plex, buy the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus . Its 12th-gen Intel chip has QuickSync with AV1 decode, it ships with 10GbE, and it takes any drive. Every pick in this table was in stock on Amazon US when we checked, and every one except the Synology transcodes in hardware.

 None of these units sat in our rack for a month of streaming, and we will not pretend otherwise. Competing guides quote “10 simultaneous 4K streams” figures lifted from a years-old Plex PassMark rule of thumb. That rule says nothing about Jellyfin, HDR tone mapping or AV1. Jasper Lake handles HEVC 10-bit but has no AV1 at all, and Jellyfin is winding down its QuickSync path on Linux.

 Intel N95 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus Alder Lake-N Yes (16 EU) Yes / Yes Yes / No Supported, 12th-gen N series 
 Intel N100 UGREEN DXP2800 Alder Lake-N Yes (24 EU) Yes / Yes Yes / No Named in the Jellyfin recommended list 
 Core i3-N305 TerraMaster F4-425 Pro (older units), F4-424 Pro Alder Lake-N Yes (32 EU) Yes / Yes Yes / No Supported, 12th-gen N series 
 Intel N150, Core 3 N350 TerraMaster F4-425 Pro (N350 version) Twin Lake Yes (24 / 32 EU) Yes / Yes* Yes / No* Supported, 12th gen or newer N series 
 Pentium Gold 8505 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Alder Lake Yes (48 EU) Yes / Yes Yes / No Supported, Gen 12 graphics 
 Core i5-1235U UGREEN DXP6800 Pro, DXP8800 Plus Alder Lake Yes (Iris Xe, 80 EU) Yes / Yes Yes / No Supported, two codec engines 
 Celeron N5095 QNAP TS-664 Jasper Lake Yes Yes / Yes No / No Linux QSV being deprecated, VA-API fallback 
 AMD Ryzen V1500B Synology DS925+ Not Intel No iGPU No No CPU transcoding only 
 Intel’s media driver lists Alder Lake-N by name but not Twin Lake. The starred N150 and N350 cells assume the same Gen 12 media block the rest of the N-series family shares. No chip in this table encodes AV1: the Jellyfin docs put AV1 encode on Arc graphics and Meteor Lake or newer. So any NAS here that advertises “AV1” means decode only, which is the half that matters when a client cannot play the file.
 Read the Jasper Lake row twice. The Jellyfin Intel hardware acceleration docs say Ice Lake, Jasper Lake and Elkhart Lake “are losing support for QSV on Linux” because Intel deprecated the MediaSDK runtime. They tell buyers to pick newer hardware. VA-API keeps those chips transcoding, and Jasper Lake also needs the i915 GuC setting for low-power encoding, so it works but carries more setup and less runway.
 HDR to SDR tone mapping runs in hardware on every Intel chip here, because they all decode HEVC 10-bit. Intel iGPUs also have no cap on simultaneous encode sessions, unlike consumer NVIDIA cards.
 Best overall for Jellyfin and Plex: UGREEN DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus covers every box a Jellyfin buyer needs to tick without a trade-off you’ll feel in year two. Its Pentium Gold 8505 is a 12th-gen Alder Lake chip with 48-EU UHD graphics, so QuickSync decodes AV1 and handles HEVC 10-bit with hardware tone mapping. It ships with 8GB of DDR5 (expandable to 64GB), four SATA bays plus two M.2 NVMe slots, and both a 10GbE and a 2.5GbE port.
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: 4-bay, Pentium Gold 8505 with QuickSync, 10GbE and 2.5GbE, no drive lock. Image: UGREEN. 
 UGREEN ships Jellyfin as an App Center package on its Intel models, so there is no container to wire up by hand. UGOS Pro accepts any CMR drive and any NVMe with no compatibility list. If you outgrow the vendor OS, the x86 board boots TrueNAS SCALE or Unraid. It sells for about $630 to $660; check the live price .
 Buy it for files, backups, a few containers and a transcoding media server in one chassis. Pass on it if you want the Synology DSM ecosystem, or if two bays are honestly enough, in which case the DXP2800 below costs about $250 less.
 Best value QuickSync NAS: TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 The F4-425 Plus is the cheapest four-bay here that still decodes AV1 in hardware. Intel ARK lists its N95 as a four-core Alder Lake-N part with 16-EU UHD graphics and QuickSync. That puts it in the 12th-gen N series Jellyfin points low-power buyers toward. TerraMaster pairs it with 8GB of DDR4, four SATA bays, three M.2 NVMe slots and two 5GbE ports, and rates its transcoding engine for H.264 and H.265 up to 4K at 60fps.
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus: 4-bay, Intel N95 with QuickSync, three M.2 slots and dual 5GbE. Image: TerraMaster. 
 Graphics muscle is where it gives ground. Sixteen execution units is the smallest iGPU in this guide, a third of the DXP4800 Plus, so a household with several remote viewers tone-mapping 4K HDR at once will hit its ceiling first. Intel also rates the N95 for single-channel memory up to 16GB, so treat it as a media and backup box rather than a VM host. At about $510 it undercuts the UGREEN four-bay by roughly $120; check the live price .
 Buy it if one or two people stream at a time and you’d rather put the savings toward drives. Look elsewhere if you need 10GbE on one port, plan to run a pile of containers, or prefer the larger app catalogues of UGOS Pro, DSM or QTS over TerraMaster TOS.
 Best budget NAS for Jellyfin: UGREEN DXP2800
 The DXP2800 runs the Intel N100, the exact chip the Jellyfin hardware selection guide names as a recommended iGPU. That makes it the safest cheap entry into hardware transcoding. Its 24-EU graphics decode AV1 and HEVC 10-bit, and the box pairs two SATA bays with two M.2 NVMe slots, 8GB of DDR5 (expandable to 16GB) and a 2.5GbE port.
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800: 2-bay, Intel N100 with QuickSync, 2.5GbE. Image: UGREEN. 
 Cheap two-bays usually force a compromise here. The Synology DS225+ uses an Intel chip whose GPU driver Synology reportedly removed, so Synology Community users report it transcoding on the CPU. The DXP2800 avoids that and runs about $370 to $390; check the live price . Two bays fill faster than people expect, though. A mirrored pair gives you the space of one drive, so if your library is already past a few terabytes, a four-bay pick saves a second purchase. Our 2-bay NAS guide compares it with the other small boxes.
 Best for Plex with PCIe expansion: QNAP TS-664
 The TS-664 is the pick when Plex, not Jellyfin, is the media server and you want room to grow. Its Celeron N5095 is a Jasper Lake chip with QuickSync. The Plex support article on hardware streaming says NAS users need “JasperLake or better” to transcode to HEVC reliably, so the N5095 clears that bar. It ships with 8GB of RAM (16GB maximum), six SATA bays, two M.2 slots, two 2.5GbE ports, HDMI at 4K 60Hz and a PCIe Gen3 slot for a 10GbE card later.
 QNAP TS-664: 6-bay, Celeron N5095 with QuickSync and a PCIe Gen3 slot for 10GbE. Image: QNAP. 
 For Jellyfin this is the weakest Intel pick on the page. Jasper Lake has no AV1 decode, its Linux QSV path is the one Jellyfin is retiring, and QTS has no official Jellyfin package, so it runs through Container Station or a community package. At about $800 it also costs more than the DXP4800 Plus with built-in 10GbE; check the live price . Choose it for six bays and Plex, not for a long-lived Jellyfin server.
 Best for the DSM ecosystem: Synology DS925+
 The DS925+ cannot transcode video in hardware at all, because its AMD Ryzen V1500B has no integrated GPU. Every Jellyfin or Plex transcode lands on four CPU cores, which is fine for direct play to a capable client and poor for anything else. It earns a place for DSM, still the most polished NAS software, plus ECC memory and Synology’s backup suite.
 Synology DiskStation DS925+: 4-bay, AMD V1500B, DSM software, ECC RAM, no hardware transcoding. Image: Synology. 
 DSM 7.3 (October 2025) restored full support for third-party hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs. Creating an M.2 NVMe storage pool still requires drives on the Synology compatibility list. The box ships with 4GB of ECC RAM (32GB maximum), which fills quickly once containers start, and runs about $770; check the live price .
 If your clients direct-play everything, it works. Our Synology NAS guide covers the rest of the range and why owners of the Intel DS225+ and DS425+ report the same transcoding problem.
 Plex Pass pricing versus free Jellyfin
 A new lifetime Plex Pass went from $249.99 to $749.99 on July 1, 2026, according to the Plex pricing announcement . The same change added a 5-Year pass at $249.99 and left monthly and annual pricing unchanged (reported at $6.99 and $69.99). Three Plex rules shape a NAS purchase:
 Hardware-accelerated streaming in Plex still requires an active Plex Pass on the server.
 Remote playback of your own video has required Plex Pass or a Remote Watch Pass ($2.99 a month) since April 29, 2025.
 Plex does not support hardware-accelerated streaming inside a virtual machine, so run it in Docker or natively on the NAS.
 Jellyfin charges nothing for hardware transcoding, remote access or extra users, so the NAS is the whole bill. The lifetime pass alone now costs more than the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus. If your household already pays for Plex Pass, every Intel box here serves it well; if you’re starting fresh, Jellyfin on the DXP4800 Plus or DXP2800 avoids the subscription entirely.
 Container settings that keep QuickSync working
 The Jellyfin hardware selection guide warns that prebuilt NAS appliances can make third-party apps hard to install. The usual failure is a container that never sees the GPU, so every stream falls back to the CPU without an error. For the official jellyfin/jellyfin image on an Intel NAS, the Jellyfin Intel docs set three conditions:
 The container has the render node /dev/dri/renderD128 passed through from the host.
 The container runs with the render group ID of the host added (some releases use video instead).
 QSV or VA-API is selected under Dashboard, Playback, Transcoding, with the decode codecs your chip supports ticked.
 Kernel version is the other trap: the same docs note that 12th and 13th-gen Intel graphics need Linux kernel 6.2 or newer. That matters if you swap the vendor OS for an older distro. If you’d rather skip the appliance software entirely, our Jellyfin media server build uses an N150 board, and pairing any of these boxes with a streaming device that direct-plays cuts how often the NAS transcodes at all.
 Drives cost more than the box
 Every NAS here ships empty, and in 2026 the drives are usually the bigger bill. Four WD Red Plus 10TB drives, the value CMR pick in our best NAS hard drives guide , run about $460 each, so roughly $1,840 for a set, which is more than any four-bay on this page. Buy CMR, never SMR: the CMR vs SMR explainer shows how SMR drives stall RAID rebuilds. Expect both drive and RAM prices to keep moving while the memory and storage shortage lasts, which is also why the RAM a box ships with matters more than its upgrade ceiling.
 Black Friday NAS pricing to watch
 Black Friday falls on November 27, 2026 and Cyber Monday on November 30, and the NAS listings above already sit below their list prices. On the day we checked, Amazon showed the DXP4800 Plus, the DXP2800 and the DS925+ each about 13% to 14% under the list price on the listing. The F4-425 Plus showed a bigger cut against its Amazon list price, but TerraMaster’s own store listed it lower than that and out of stock, so Amazon was the only place we found it buyable. Before you call a holiday price a deal, check these conditions:
 The holiday price beats the current price band in the table above, not only the struck-through list price.
 The listing is the same diskless model and RAM configuration as the pick, not a bundle or a lower-RAM variant.
 The seller is the brand or Amazon, so the warranty and returns are straightforward.
 Drives tend to see the deeper cuts. Our Black Friday NAS and drive deals page tracks both through Cyber Monday.
 Which NAS fits your library
 Bay count and stream count decide this more than brand. Start from how much media you already own and how many people watch at once:
 One or two viewers, a library under about 8TB: the UGREEN DXP2800, or more two-bays in our 2-bay roundup .
 A family library with room to grow on a budget: the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus.
 A family library plus containers and fast copies from a desktop: the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, with more price tiers in the 4-bay NAS guide .
 Plex with six bays and a PCIe slot: the QNAP TS-664.
 A large library or several remote viewers: an eight-bay from our 8-bay NAS picks .
 Photo libraries run on the same boxes, and our NAS for Immich guide covers the extra RAM that machine learning needs. Live TV adds an HDHomeRun tuner for Plex and Jellyfin , and if none of the appliances fit, the DIY versus prebuilt comparison works through the costs of building your own.
 Pairs with Best UPS for Homelab and NAS (2026): Pure Sine Picks + NUT 
 Best Synology Alternatives: UGREEN vs QNAP vs UniFi UNAS vs DIY 
 ZimaCube 2 NAS Guide: Drives, RAID, Review Data 
 Pre-purchase transcode checklist
 Run these checks against any NAS listing before you buy, including ones not on this page. Each one is a condition the box must meet, and each traces to a source you can open yourself:
 The CPU is an Intel chip whose ARK page shows Intel Quick Sync Video as Yes.
 The Intel codename is Alder Lake, Alder Lake-N, Twin Lake or newer, not Jasper Lake, Elkhart Lake or Ice Lake, if Jellyfin is the main server.
 The chip decodes HEVC 10-bit, so HDR to SDR tone mapping runs on the GPU.
 The chip decodes AV1 if any of your files or downloads use it.
 The vendor ships Jellyfin as a package, or the NAS runs Docker with access to /dev/dri .
 The box ships with at least 8GB of RAM, because upgrades cost several times more than they did in June 2026.
 The listing is sold new by the brand or Amazon and matches the exact model number on the spec page from the maker.
 The drives you plan to fill it with are CMR and are priced into the same budget as the box.

 Quick Summary (TL;DR): 
For a NAS Price AliExpress price that will regularly transcode Plex or Jellyfin streams, prioritise a modern Intel processor with Quick Sync Video rather than simply buying the NAS AliExpress price with the fastest CPU. Our current shortlist is led Price by the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Price with its 12th-generation Intel 8505, 48-EU iGPU, 8GB DDR5 expandable to 64GB and built-in 10GbE. The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus is a strong lower-power alternative with the newer Intel N150 , 16GB DDR5, dual 5GbE and an explicitly advertised hardware transcoding engine. The QNAP TS-464 remains one of the safest mature-platform choices: its Jasper Lake N5095 is not powerful by current CPU standards, but QNAP explicitly supports hardware-accelerated transcoding and Plex currently says NAS AliExpress price users need Jasper Lake or newer for reliable HEVC-output transcoding. The Synology DS425+ has Intel Quick Sync, but its older Gemini Lake Refresh J4125 falls below that current Plex recommendation, so we would choose it mainly for DSM and Direct Play rather than as a new transcoding-first purchase. Plex hardware acceleration requires an active Plex Pass; Jellyfin hardware acceleration does not, but both require the iGPU to be exposed correctly—especially in Docker. If most clients Direct Play your files, transcoding performance matters far less and storage capacity, software ecosystem and network speed should drive the NAS decision instead.
 Best NAS for Plex and Jellyfin Hardware Transcoding: Shortlist
 NAS CPU / media hardware Why it stands out Main limitation 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Intel 8505, 48-EU UHD, Quick Sync Strongest overall compute, 64GB RAM ceiling, 10GbE UGOS Pro ecosystem is younger than QNAP/Synology 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus Intel N150 , 24-EU Intel Graphics, Quick Sync Modern low-power media engine, 16GB RAM, dual 5GbE 32GB RAM ceiling; M.2 slots are PCIe 3.0 x1 
 QNAP TS-464 Intel N5095 Jasper Lake, UHD, Quick Sync Mature Plex/QTS platform, explicit HW transcoding support, PCIe expansion 16GB official RAM ceiling; older CPU 
 QNAP TS-664 Same N5095 platform Same media engine with six HDD bays No compute advantage over TS-464 
 Synology DS425+ Intel J4125, UHD 600, Quick Sync DSM ecosystem, Direct Play, light legacy transcoding Older Gemini Lake Refresh; below Plex’s current Jasper Lake HEVC-output recommendation 
 The Most Important Rule: Buy the Video Engine, Not the CPU Benchmark
 Video transcoding is different from general CPU work.
 A powerful CPU can transcode in software, but modern Intel processors contain dedicated fixed-function video hardware through Intel Quick Sync Video . Plex and Jellyfin can use that hardware to decode and encode video while leaving most CPU resources available for the rest of the NAS .
 That is why an Intel N5095 NAS can be a better Plex purchase than a more powerful AMD Ryzen NAS that has no supported integrated media engine.
 Why Hardware Transcoding Matters
 Transcoding happens when the client cannot play the original file directly or when the requested stream must be changed.
 Remote bandwidth is lower than the source bitrate.
 The client does not support the source codec.
 The client requests a lower resolution.
 The audio format is incompatible.
 Subtitles must be burned into the picture.
 HDR video must be converted to SDR.
 Plex notes that transcoding is CPU-intensive and that hardware acceleration can make high-quality HEVC/4K conversion smoother while reducing the load and power consumption of the main CPU.
 Direct Play Is Still Better Than Transcoding
 The best transcode is the one you do not need.
 If your TV, streaming box, phone or browser can play the original container, codec, audio and subtitle combination, Plex or Jellyfin can use Direct Play .
 Direct Play requires very little server compute.
 A large 4K remux can still require substantial network bandwidth, but the NAS CPU is mostly reading the file and sending it to the client.
 If nearly everything in your home Direct Plays, spend money on:
 More drive bays.
 Larger HDDs.
 Better backup.
 2.5GbE or 10GbE where useful.
 Better client devices.
 rather than buying an expensive NAS only for a more powerful transcoder.
 Plex Hardware Acceleration Requires Plex Pass
 Plex currently requires an active Plex Pass subscription for normal hardware-accelerated streaming.
 When enabled, Plex can use supported Intel Quick Sync hardware for video decoding and encoding.
 In Plex:
 Settings
→ Server
→ Transcoder
→ Show Advanced
→ Use hardware acceleration when available 
 During playback, the Plex Dashboard should show (hw) beside the transcoded video path when hardware acceleration is actually working.
 Jellyfin Hardware Acceleration Does Not Need a Paid Licence
 Jellyfin supports several hardware-acceleration methods, including:
 Intel Quick Sync Video (QSV).
 Intel/AMD VA-API on Linux.
 NVIDIA NVENC/NVDEC.
 AMD AMF on Windows.
 For Intel NAS hardware, QSV or VA-API are the important choices.
 Jellyfin can accelerate multiple stages of the pipeline, including decoding, deinterlacing, scaling, HDR tone mapping and encoding when the hardware/software combination supports them.
 Best Overall: UGREEN DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus uses Intel’s 12th-generation Pentium Gold 8505.
 5 CPU cores / 6 threads.
 Up to 4.4GHz.
 Intel UHD Graphics.
 48 graphics execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 One multi-format codec engine.
 8GB DDR5 included.
 Up to 64GB RAM.
 1 × 10GbE + 1 × 2.5GbE.
 4 SATA bays + 2 M.2 slots.
 The 8505 is far newer than the J4125 and N5095 class and has substantially more general CPU headroom than either.
 That matters when Plex/Jellyfin shares the NAS with:
 Docker applications.
 Immich.
 Databases.
 Home Assistant services.
 Download automation.
 Media indexing.
 The built-in 10GbE port is unnecessary for one ordinary media stream, but useful when the same NAS also serves workstation backups, large file transfers or several clients.
 UGREEN’s main trade-off is software maturity. UGOS Pro has developed quickly, but QNAP and Synology have longer-established native NAS ecosystems.
 We cover the exact current UGREEN Plex/Jellyfin deployment and acceleration checks separately in Plex and Jellyfin Hardware Transcoding on UGREEN NASync .
 Best Modern Value Alternative: TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 The F4-425 Plus uses Intel’s newer N150 processor.
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 Up to 3.6GHz.
 6W processor base power.
 Intel Graphics with 24 execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 16GB DDR5 included.
 Up to 32GB RAM.
 2 × 5GbE.
 3 × M.2 PCIe 3.0 x1 slots.
 TerraMaster explicitly lists hardware transcoding for H.264, H.265, MPEG-4 and VC-1 on the F4-425 Plus, with the current product page advertising an 8K@60fps transcoding engine.
 The N150 is also newer than Plex’s “Jasper Lake or better” requirement for reliable HEVC-output transcoding on NAS.
 This combination makes the F4-425 Plus particularly attractive when you want:
 A modern Intel media engine.
 Plenty of RAM out of the box.
 Fast networking.
 Four HDD bays.
 Docker/Jellyfin/Plex capability.
 Its general CPU is less capable than the UGREEN 8505, but a transcoding-first NAS often benefits more from the media engine than from extra CPU cores.
 Best Mature QNAP Option: TS-464
 The QNAP TS-464 uses Intel’s Celeron N5095.
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 Up to 2.9GHz.
 Intel UHD Graphics.
 16 graphics execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 8GB DDR4 on the current 8G model.
 Up to 16GB officially supported RAM.
 2 × 2.5GbE.
 2 × M.2 PCIe Gen3 x1.
 PCIe Gen3 x2 expansion slot.
 The key detail is the CPU generation: N5095 is Jasper Lake .
 Plex currently says NAS users need Jasper Lake or better to reliably transcode to HEVC output. That keeps the TS-464 relevant even though its CPU is now old compared with an 8505 or N150.
 QNAP also explicitly lists hardware-accelerated transcoding as supported on the TS-464.
 Its strongest reasons to buy are:
 Mature QTS software.
 Container Station.
 Virtualization Station.
 Established Plex deployment history.
 PCIe expansion.
 HDMI 2.1 output.
 The main limitation is the 16GB official RAM ceiling. That matters more for a large home-lab stack than for Plex itself.
 Need Six Bays? QNAP TS-664 Uses the Same Media Platform
 The TS-664 uses the same N5095 CPU, graphics and 16GB memory ceiling as the TS-464.
 It therefore does not provide more transcoding compute.
 What it gives you is two additional SATA bays, which can be much more useful for a large movie/TV library.
 Choose TS-664 instead of TS-464 when the problem is media capacity , not transcoding speed.
 Best DSM Option: Synology DS425+—with a Major Caveat
 The DS425+ uses Intel’s Celeron J4125.
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 2.0GHz base / 2.7GHz burst.
 Intel UHD Graphics 600.
 12 execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 2GB DDR4 included.
 Up to 6GB total RAM.
 1 × 2.5GbE + 1 × 1GbE.
 The DS425+ therefore does have an Intel hardware video engine.
 The problem is generation. Intel identifies J4125 as Gemini Lake Refresh , while Plex currently recommends Jasper Lake or better for reliable HEVC-output transcoding on NAS.
 That makes the DS425+ reasonable for:
 Direct Play.
 Older H.264-heavy libraries.
 Occasional compatible hardware transcoding.
 Buyers who prioritise DSM over media-server performance.
 It is not our first choice for a new NAS bought specifically around modern HEVC transcoding.
 Why We Would Not Choose the Synology DS925+ for Transcoding
 The DS925+ is a stronger storage/server platform than the DS425+ in several areas: ECC RAM, 32GB memory support, eight CPU threads and expansion to nine bays.
 But its Ryzen V1500B does not provide an Intel Quick Sync media engine.
 For backups, Docker and storage growth, DS925+ can be the better NAS. For Plex/Jellyfin hardware transcoding, the older Intel DS425+ has the more useful architecture.
 A Fast AMD NAS Is Not Automatically a Fast Transcoding NAS
 This lesson extends beyond Synology.
 High-performance AMD systems such as the ASUSTOR Lockerstor 4 Gen3 can have much stronger CPU, ECC RAM and networking than an N5095 NAS.
 But if the processor does not expose a supported video encode/decode engine, Plex may need to use CPU software transcoding.
 Jellyfin supports AMD hardware acceleration when a suitable AMD GPU/APU is present, but not every Ryzen Embedded CPU includes the required graphics engine.
 HEVC Output Changed the CPU Generation Requirement
 Plex’s current hardware-accelerated streaming documentation includes an important NAS-specific line: Jasper Lake or better is required to reliably transcode to HEVC output .
 This matters because older NAS buying guides often treat any Quick Sync processor as equivalent.
 They are not.
 CPU Generation Current Plex HEVC-output position 
 J4125 Gemini Lake Refresh Older than current Jasper Lake recommendation 
 N5095 Jasper Lake Meets stated minimum generation 
 N150 Twin Lake Newer than stated minimum 
 Intel 8505 Alder Lake Newer than stated minimum 
 HEVC Encoding in Plex Is Still Experimental
 As of the current Plex transcoder documentation, HEVC video encoding is still marked experimental .
 Plex warns that HEVC encoding uses more resources and will generally support fewer concurrent streams than H.264.
 Do not buy a NAS based on an assumption such as “this will always transcode six 4K streams to HEVC”. Plex software, drivers, source files, HDR processing and subtitles can all change the result.
 HDR Tone Mapping Is a Separate Requirement
 Converting HDR video to SDR can add substantial processing work.
 Plex hardware tone mapping requires supported server software and compatible hardware. Plex currently notes an Intel Kaby Lake-or-newer requirement for relevant hardware-accelerated tone-mapping paths.
 Jellyfin supports hardware-accelerated HDR10/HLG tone mapping and supports Intel VPP tone mapping through QSV/VA-API on Linux.
 If your library is mostly 4K HDR remuxes and remote clients frequently need SDR, test this exact path—not simply “4K transcoding”.
 Subtitles Can Break an Otherwise Easy Transcode
 Subtitle format matters.
 Text subtitles such as SRT are often easier for clients to render directly. Image-based subtitles such as PGS may force subtitle burn-in depending on the client and playback path.
 Burn-in can move parts of the pipeline back to CPU processing and dramatically change performance.
 This is why “How many 4K streams?” is usually the wrong benchmark question.
 Docker Hardware Transcoding Works—but the Device Must Be Passed Through
 Plex explicitly supports hardware acceleration inside Docker when the host exposes a supported Intel Quick Sync device to the container.
 On a Linux-based Intel NAS, this normally means exposing the relevant /dev/dri device into the container and ensuring the container has the correct permissions.
 Jellyfin similarly requires access to the host’s GPU device and the appropriate QSV/VA-API configuration.
 If the container cannot see the iGPU, buying a Quick Sync CPU provides no hardware-transcoding benefit.
 Do Not Put Plex in a VM Expecting Quick Sync Automatically
 Plex’s current documentation says hardware-accelerated streaming is not supported inside ordinary virtual machines because the required low-level video hardware is not normally exposed to the guest.
 Advanced hypervisors can support PCIe/iGPU passthrough in other architectures, but that is a separate design problem.
 For an appliance NAS, Docker/native Plex is usually the cleaner hardware-transcoding path.
 RAM Matters Less for Transcoding Than People Think
 Plex itself does not need 64GB RAM to transcode video.
 Large memory capacity matters when the NAS also hosts:
 Immich.
 Nextcloud.
 Several databases.
 VMs.
 Large Docker stacks.
 RAM-based transcode temporary storage.
 For a pure Plex/Jellyfin box, modern Intel media hardware matters more than a huge RAM ceiling.
 SSD Cache Will Not Make Video Transcoding Faster by Magic
 A modern HDD can read one large movie file far faster than required for normal playback.
 SSD/NVMe is more useful for:
 Plex/Jellyfin metadata.
 Thumbnail databases.
 Transcode temporary files.
 Docker application data.
 Large multi-user metadata workloads.
 Store the bulk movie library on HDD unless silence, size or a specific high-performance workload justifies flash.
 1GbE Is Enough for Many Media Servers
 One Gigabit Ethernet connection can deliver roughly 100MB/s-plus of real application throughput under good conditions.
 That is far more than one ordinary compressed 4K stream needs.
 2.5GbE or 10GbE becomes valuable when the NAS also handles:
 Large workstation transfers.
 Multiple simultaneous users.
 Backups while media is streaming.
 Video editing.
 Several high-bitrate streams plus other NAS workloads.
 Do not buy a 10GbE NAS solely because you plan to watch one movie at a time.
 When a Mini PC Plus NAS Is Better
 If you need very strong transcoding but also want a large, long-lived storage array, separate compute and storage can be the better architecture.
 Intel mini PC 
Plex / Jellyfin / Quick Sync
 │
 2.5/10GbE
 │
NAS with large HDD array 
 This lets you upgrade the media-server CPU without replacing the NAS enclosure and drive array.
 Our dedicated troubleshooting/buying article covers this decision: Plex Server vs NAS Storage: Which Component Should You Upgrade First? .
 Practical Buying Matrix
 Your priority Best fit Why 
 Best overall four-bay transcoding/home-server mix UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Alder Lake 8505, Quick Sync, 64GB RAM, 10GbE 
 Modern low-power media NAS TerraMaster F4-425 Plus N150 Quick Sync, 16GB RAM, explicit HW transcoding 
 Mature QTS/Plex ecosystem QNAP TS-464 Jasper Lake Quick Sync, explicit HW transcoding, QTS 
 Six-bay Plex library QNAP TS-664 Same media engine with more HDD capacity 
 DSM + mostly Direct Play Synology DS425+ DSM ecosystem and Intel Quick Sync 
 Modern HEVC-output transcoding 8505 / N150 / N5095 class Meets or exceeds Plex’s Jasper Lake generation guidance

 Inclusion requires a manufacturer-verified Intel iGPU (Quick Sync). ARM models and iGPU-less Ryzen models — including current Synology Plus units — are excluded because they cannot hardware-transcode.
 Why Quick Sync decides this purchase
 Plex playback comes in two modes. Direct play hands the file to the client untouched — nearly free for the server, and any NAS can do it. Transcoding re-encodes video on the fly because the client cannot handle the original — a phone on hotel Wi-Fi, a TV that predates HEVC, a burned-in subtitle track — and done in software it saturates a NAS-class CPU with a single 4K stream. Intel's Quick Sync is dedicated silicon that does the same job at a fraction of the load: the modest N100 in a budget UGREEN handles 4K HEVC transcodes that would flatten a far more expensive CPU without an iGPU.
 This is why the brand landscape for Plex looks nothing like the general NAS market. UGREEN's entire Intel lineup qualifies — the value king's Quick Sync coverage is total, from the 2-bay DXP2800 to the 8-bay DXP8800 Plus. QNAP's TS-464 and TS-664 built their reputations on exactly this workload. TerraMaster's Intel boxes qualify at the lowest prices in the table. And Synology — the biggest name in NAS — is absent entirely, because its current Ryzen-based Plus models ship no iGPU. For a transcoding household, the "which brand" debate collapses to the live prices above.
 One licensing note belongs in the budget: Plex gates hardware transcoding behind Plex Pass. Jellyfin, the open-source alternative, uses the same Quick Sync hardware for free and runs on every device in the table. Either way, the hardware you are buying is identical — an Intel iGPU and enough bays for the library.
 Picks by budget and library size
 Starter (2-bay Intel). The UGREEN DXP2800 and TerraMaster F2-425 put real transcoding into mirror-sized boxes. Right for a first server, a single-TV household with remote streaming needs, or a bedroom deployment. The constraint is capacity, not compute — a mirror holds one drive's worth of media, and libraries grow. Buy this tier knowing its ceiling, or skip ahead one.
 Mainstream (4-bay Intel). The center of gravity, and where our best-for-Plex decision card on the hub points: RAID 5 capacity for a serious library plus transcode headroom for a family's worth of simultaneous streams. The QNAP TS-464 is the category's reference box (PCIe for future 10GbE included); UGREEN's 4-bays undercut it with newer silicon; the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro brings an 8-core i3 at a price that reads like a typo. Today's cheapest qualifying 4-bay is the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 4-Bay at $632.98 .
 Heavy (6-8 bay Intel). Tens of terabytes, multiple 4K remuxes, several concurrent users: UGREEN's DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus pair 10-core i5 chips with dual 10GbE, and QNAP's TS-664 extends the TS platform to RAID 6 territory. At this tier the drives dominate the budget — see the 6-bay and 8-bay guides for the array planning, and the NAS Builder for complete build costs at live prices.
 Sizing the library, honestly
 Media libraries have a one-way ratchet: a 4K remux runs 50-80GB, a Blu-ray rip 25-40GB, a full TV series in 1080p easily 100GB+, and nothing ever gets deleted. A hundred-film collection with a modest TV habit crosses 10TB without trying; enthusiasts cross 50TB with enthusiasm. Work backwards from three years of collecting, add RAID overhead, and you have your drive budget — which is where the real money goes. At today's prices, the cheapest in-stock 20TB drive ( WD , $630.00 ) puts a 60TB-usable RAID 5 library at $2,520.00 in drives alone before the enclosure.
 Drive guidance for this workload is mercifully simple: big CMR drives, nothing exotic. Streaming is sequential reads — the thing spinning drives are best at — so NAS-class or recertified enterprise drives from the live per-terabyte rankings are the right buy, and SSD caching adds little to a workload this linear. Put the flash budget into one more spinning drive instead. The one non-negotiable is CMR over SMR — rebuilds on a media array full of large drives are exactly where SMR's pathological write behavior hurts most.
 Protection strategy differs from a document server, and honestly so: most Plex libraries are re-acquirable, which changes the backup math. RAID 5 or 6 protects the weeks of curation time a rebuild-from-scratch would cost, and that is usually protection enough for the media itself — but the Plex metadata database, watch states and collections are genuinely irreplaceable, tiny, and worth backing up on a schedule to any external target. Protect the library with RAID, protect the curation with backups, and spend the money saved on capacity.
 Network, clients and the first evening
 Plex is kinder to networks than spec-sheet shoppers assume: a 4K remux streams at 40-100Mbps, so gigabit Ethernet carries several simultaneous streams and even good Wi-Fi handles one. The faster ports on these boxes earn their keep during library loading and file management, not playback — which means 2.5GbE is genuinely sufficient for a pure Plex box, and 10GbE is a file-transfer luxury. Wire the NAS to the router if humanly possible; the flakiest Plex setups are almost always Wi-Fi-attached servers, not underpowered ones.
 The first evening's checklist, in order: update the NAS OS and install Plex from the official package source; store the config on the SSD if your model has M.2 (metadata on flash makes browsing snappy even when the library sleeps on spinning drives); point Plex at your media folders with the recommended naming scheme; enable hardware transcoding in Plex settings (it is off by default even on Quick Sync boxes); and set remote access through Plex's relay rather than port-forwarding the NAS itself. Then play the ugliest file you own on the weakest client you own — if that transcode is smooth, everything else will be.
 One honest scope note: this page covers NAS appliances, and a used mini-PC with an Intel chip plus a USB enclosure can undercut all of them for pure transcoding duty. What the NAS buys you is the storage half done properly — RAID, snapshots, drive management, one box instead of a science project. Buyers tempted by the DIY route should price it against the live table above with drives included; the gap is usually smaller than expected, and the appliance keeps weekends free.
 Frequently asked questions
 What is the best NAS for Plex in 2026? For most Plex households: the cheapest in-stock Intel-iGPU 4-bay, currently the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 4-Bay at $632.98 in our live table. It hardware-transcodes 4K, holds a RAID 5 library, and leaves headroom for growth. Budget setups can start on an Intel 2-bay; heavy libraries step up to the 6- and 8-bay Intel models. Every price above is live.
 Do I really need hardware transcoding for Plex? If every client always direct-plays your exact formats — same codec, container and subtitles the TV supports natively — no. In practice, remote streams, phones, bandwidth limits, burned-in subtitles and older TVs all force transcodes, and one software-transcoded 4K stream will bring a NAS CPU to its knees. A Quick Sync iGPU turns that same transcode into a light workload. Buying transcode capability is buying insurance against how your library actually gets watched.
 Does Plex hardware transcoding require Plex Pass? Yes — hardware-accelerated transcoding is a Plex Pass feature. Factor the subscription (or lifetime pass) into the build budget, or consider Jellyfin, which is free and uses the same Intel Quick Sync hardware. Every iGPU model in our table accelerates both.
 Why are Synology NAS absent from this page? Current Synology Plus models use AMD Ryzen embedded CPUs with no integrated GPU, so they cannot hardware-transcode — they only qualify for direct-play libraries. This page lists devices we have verified as transcode-capable. If you want DSM anyway for a direct-play setup, the Synology brand page covers the lineup with live prices.
 How many drives does a Plex NAS need? Media libraries grow monotonically — nobody deletes movies — so buy bays for the library you will have in three years. A 4-bay in RAID 5 (three drives usable) is the mainstream answer; serious collections go six bays and RAID 6. Spinning drives are the right medium: sequential streaming is what hard drives do best, and per-terabyte pricing crushes SSDs for this workload.
 Can a cheap ARM NAS run Plex at all? It can run the server and direct-play to one or two clients, and for a disciplined single-TV household that genuinely suffices. What it cannot do is transcode meaningfully — one incompatible client turns playback into a slideshow. The price gap between ARM boxes and the cheapest Intel-iGPU models in our live table is modest; for Plex it is the highest-value money in the build.

 Why the CPU decides a Plex NAS
 A NAS is only a good Plex server if its processor can hardware-transcode, and that comes down to one thing: an Intel iGPU with Quick Sync. Intel-powered NAS units (Celeron, Pentium and the newer N-series) carry that engine and transcode H.264 and HEVC efficiently. ARM-based units (Rockchip, ARM Cortex) and the AMD Ryzen chips in several newer Synology Plus models have no iGPU, so Plex either direct-plays only or falls back to slow CPU software transcoding that stutters under load.
 This is the trap on the current market: some of the newest, most expensive NAS units are worse for Plex than older, cheaper ones, because the vendor moved to an AMD Ryzen platform with no integrated graphics. A DS923+ or DS925+ is a fine file server but a poor transcoding Plex box, while the older DS224+ on an Intel Celeron transcodes happily. Read the CPU, not the model year.
 What each capability level gets you
 An Intel-Celeron NAS (DS224+, DS423+, TS-264, TS-464) hardware-transcodes 1080p comfortably and can manage 4K HEVC in many cases, which covers most households that occasionally transcode. The Intel N100 UGREEN units (DXP2800, DXP4800) use the same modern Quick Sync as the budget builds on this site, so they add efficient 4K HEVC decode and light 4K transcoding. The Pentium Gold 8505 in the DXP4800 Plus steps that up further.
 An ARM or AMD-Ryzen NAS is a direct-play machine. If every client can play your files natively, it streams them untouched and resolution does not matter. The moment a client forces a transcode, though, these units crawl. So the honest rule is: buy Intel if you will ever transcode, and only consider ARM or Ryzen if you are certain your whole setup direct-plays or you will run Plex on separate hardware.
 Then fit the right drives
 Once the transcoding question is settled, a Plex NAS lives or dies on storage, and the value metric is price per terabyte. Fit NAS-rated CMR drives sized to the bays, and use the device drive pages to see the exact models and live prices for your unit. A media pool is backed up and tolerant, so recertified enterprise drives and shucked externals often give the lowest cost per terabyte, which the shucking tracker shows live.
 If your chosen NAS turns out to be ARM or Ryzen but you still want real transcoding, the split build is the answer: keep the NAS for storage and run Plex on a small Intel mini PC beside it. That pairs cheap bulk storage with a proper Quick Sync transcoder, and it is often cheaper than buying the one high-end Intel NAS that does both.
 Before you buy
 Vendors occasionally change what their software exposes to Plex, so confirm the current firmware still gives Plex access to the iGPU on the exact model you are considering, and check that your Plex clients need transcoding at all. Many people discover that with a modern client that direct-plays, even a modest NAS is enough, and the transcoding worry was moot. When in doubt, an Intel-Celeron or N100 NAS is the safe, transcode-capable choice.

 Frequently asked questions
 What is the best NAS for Plex hardware transcoding?
 A NAS with an Intel CPU that has Quick Sync. Among tracked models that means the Synology DS224+ and DS423+ (Celeron J4125), QNAP TS-264 and TS-464 (Celeron N5095), and UGREEN DXP2800/DXP4800 (Intel N100) or DXP4800 Plus (Pentium Gold 8505). These transcode in hardware; ARM and AMD-Ryzen NAS units cannot.
 Can a Synology DS923+ transcode Plex?
 Not in hardware. The DS923+ (and DS925+, DS1525+) use an AMD Ryzen CPU with no integrated GPU, so they have no Quick Sync and cannot hardware-transcode. They direct-play fine but fall back to slow software transcoding. For transcoding on Synology, choose an older Intel-Celeron model like the DS224+ or DS423+.
 Do ARM-based NAS units work with Plex?
 Only for direct play. ARM NAS units (Rockchip, ARM Cortex) have no Quick Sync, so they cannot hardware-transcode and software-transcode very slowly. If all your clients play files natively they are fine, but any forced transcode will stutter. Buy Intel if you need transcoding.
 Is a NAS or a mini PC better for Plex transcoding?
 An Intel NAS transcodes and stores in one box, which is simplest. But a small Intel mini PC plus a NAS or DAS for storage (the split build) often gives more transcoding power per dollar and lets you pick a cheap ARM or Ryzen NAS purely for storage. Choose the all-in-one Intel NAS for simplicity, the split build for value.
 How many Plex streams can a Celeron NAS handle?
 An Intel-Celeron NAS like the DS224+ or TS-464 comfortably handles a couple of 1080p transcodes and can manage 4K HEVC in many cases, which suits most households. Heavy multi-user 4K transcoding is better served by a dedicated build with a newer Core i5 iGPU. Exact numbers depend on the source files and clients.
 What drives should I put in a Plex NAS?
 NAS-rated CMR drives sized to the bays, chosen by live price per terabyte. Because a media pool is backed up, recertified enterprise drives and shucked externals often give the lowest cost per terabyte. See the device drive page for your model and the shucking tracker for the current cheapest terabytes.

If you’re building a home lab NAS setup on a budget, one of these will fit. We also explain where Synology and TerraMaster fit at this price.
