 The ASUSTOR AS5402T packs an Intel N5105, dual 2.5GbE, and four M.2 NVMe slots into a package that costs roughly $400. It has two SATA bays. If two SATA bays plus NVMe storage cover your needs, it’s the most hardware per dollar in this range.
 CPU: Intel Celeron N5105, 4 cores and 4 threads, up to 2.9 GHz
 Memory: 4 GB DDR4 in two slots, 16 GB maximum (ASUSTOR)
 Storage: 2x 3.5”/2.5” SATA bays + 4x M.2 NVMe (PCIe 3.0 x1)
 Network and ports: 2x 2.5GbE, HDMI 2.0b, 3x USB 3.2 Gen 2
 Rated power and noise: 12.7W with disks hibernating, 22.9W in operation, and 18.6 dB with drives idle (ASUSTOR)
 The N5105 combines four Jasper Lake cores, Intel Quick Sync, and a 2.9 GHz burst clock. That’s enough for file serving, several containers, and light hardware-accelerated transcoding.
 Four M.2 NVMe slots are the standout. Install NVMe SSDs for a fast tier (Docker volumes and databases) alongside two spinning SATA drives for a slow tier (media and backups). The best 4-bay NAS models typically offer only two M.2 slots. Each slot is PCIe 3.0 x1, so the gain is latency and IOPS rather than per-drive sequential speed.
 The compromise is ADM. ASUSTOR’s software is functional, with fewer first-party apps and a smaller community than QTS or DSM, and no equivalent to Synology’s Active Backup suite. Docker is available through App Central, but expect to lean on Portainer or the command line more than on QNAP or Synology.
 Buy this if: You want Intel Quick Sync and 2.5GbE for the least money, and two SATA bays plus NVMe give you enough storage. It suits a secondary NAS, a dedicated Plex box, or an SSD-first Docker host.
 Best 4-Bay: UGREEN NASync DH4300 Plus
 The UGREEN NASync DH4300 Plus is the four-bay pick and the NAS for people who don’t want to think about NAS administration. UGOS Pro walks you through setup, the photo tools are strong, and 8 GB of RAM means light Docker containers run without an upgrade. UGREEN lists it at $439.99.
 CPU: Rockchip 8-core ARM (A76 and A55 cores), up to 2.4 GHz
 Memory: 8 GB LPDDR4X, fixed
 Storage: 4x 3.5”/2.5” SATA bays; no M.2 slots
 Network and ports: 1x 2.5GbE, USB-C, USB 3.2, 4K HDMI, NFC
 AI: 6 TOPS NPU for on-device photo recognition
 Four bays support RAID 5, and the eight ARM cores handle file serving, direct-play media, and light Docker containers. The NPU powers on-device photo recognition, including faces and objects, without sending your photos to the cloud, which matters if you’re moving off Google Photos.
 The hardware limits are real for home-lab use. With no M.2 slots, there’s no SSD caching, so all storage is SATA. The single 2.5GbE port can’t be aggregated, there’s no PCIe slot, and the 8 GB of memory is fixed. Plex hardware transcoding on Linux supports Intel Quick Sync and NVIDIA, not this ARM chip, so plan on direct play.
 UGOS Pro is young software. It supports common tasks: file sharing, photo backup, and Docker through its built-in app, which handles images, containers, and Compose projects. It lacks the depth of DSM or QTS for advanced storage layouts, logging, and permissions. UGREEN supports Docker on this model but not virtual machines, and containers need ARM64 images.
 Buy this if: You want four bays and the simplest possible setup with strong photo management. It’s a good fit for family file sharing, phone photo backup, and a few light containers. It’s the wrong pick for Plex transcoding, heavy home-lab workloads, or anyone who wants hardware upgrade paths.
 What About TerraMaster?
 TerraMaster’s current four-bay range starts with the F4-425 Plus, which TerraMaster lists at $599.99, above this guide’s ceiling. The older F4-223 no longer appears in TerraMaster’s Home/SOHO lineup, so we don’t recommend it as a new purchase. If you see one for sale, treat it as previous-generation hardware and check the warranty terms.
 What About Synology?
 Synology’s current entry four-bay Plus model is the Synology DS425+ , the successor to the DS423+. Per Synology, it has an Intel Celeron J4125 (4 cores, up to 2.7 GHz), 2 GB of DDR4 expandable to 6 GB, one 2.5GbE port plus one 1GbE port, two M.2 NVMe slots, and no PCIe slot. DSM’s backup and management tools remain the best in this class.
 We didn’t include it as a pick because we couldn’t confirm that it sells at or under $500. Check its current price. If it fits your budget, it’s the DSM choice at this level, but plan on a memory upgrade before using Docker.
 How to Choose: Buying Criteria
 CPU Architecture: Intel vs. ARM
 Intel CPUs like the ASUSTOR’s N5105 bring two big advantages for home-lab use: hardware video transcoding that Plex supports, and the broadest software compatibility, since most Docker images publish x86 builds first. ARM chips like the UGREEN’s run many containers fine, but some images lack ARM64 builds, and Plex hardware transcoding isn’t available. If you plan to run Plex for remote users or deploy a wide variety of containers, buy Intel.
 Networking: 1GbE vs. 2.5GbE
 In 2026, 2.5GbE should be the target. A single 1GbE port caps throughput at about 112 MB/s, which is fine for streaming video but a bottleneck for multi-user file access, VM storage, and large backup jobs. Both picks have at least one 2.5GbE port (about 280 MB/s), and the ASUSTOR has two for link aggregation.
 RAM: How Much Do You Actually Need?
 For basic file serving, 2 GB works. For Docker, 4 GB is the minimum and 8 GB is recommended. For more than five or six containers with databases, plan on 8 to 16 GB. The UGREEN ships with 8 GB but can’t be upgraded; the ASUSTOR starts at 4 GB and takes up to 16 GB, which matters if you add containers over time.
 Drive Bays: 2-Bay vs. 4-Bay
 Four bays support RAID 5: single-disk redundancy with 75% usable capacity. With four 8 TB drives, you get 24 TB usable. Two bays limit you to RAID 1 (mirroring) with 50% usable capacity, so two 8 TB drives give you 8 TB. The ASUSTOR AS5402T offsets its two SATA bays with four NVMe slots, but if you need bulk hard-drive storage, a four-bay unit like the DH4300 Plus is the better foundation. For more four-bay options above this budget, see our best 4-bay NAS guide.
 Expansion and Future-Proofing
 Neither pick has a PCIe expansion slot, so choose networking and drive bays for the workload you expect over the appliance’s lifetime. The ASUSTOR’s four M.2 slots offer the most internal flash flexibility; the UGREEN’s four bays favor bulk storage and simple backups.
 Bottom Line
 The ASUSTOR AS5402T , at roughly $400, is the best all-around choice, with Quick Sync, expandable memory, dual 2.5GbE, and four M.2 slots. If you need four bays and simplicity matters most, the UGREEN DH4300 Plus , listed at $439.99, is the easiest NAS to set up and live with. If you want Synology, check whether the DS425+ fits your budget before you buy; TerraMaster’s current four-bay models start above $500.
 Frequently Asked Questions

 Can a NAS under $500 handle Plex transcoding? The ASUSTOR AS5402T can, through the Intel Quick Sync engine in its N5105. Plex hardware transcoding on Linux supports Intel Quick Sync and NVIDIA, so the ARM-based UGREEN DH4300 Plus is best for direct play.
 Is 4 GB or 8 GB of RAM enough for a NAS running Docker? For a few light containers such as Pi-hole, Home Assistant, and a reverse proxy, 4 GB is workable. For Plex, multiple containers, and databases, you want at least 8 GB. The ASUSTOR ships with 4 GB and can be upgraded to 16 GB; the UGREEN ships with 8 GB but cannot be upgraded.
 Should I buy a 2-bay or 4-bay NAS under $500? A 4-bay NAS supports RAID 5, which balances single-disk redundancy and usable capacity. A 2-bay NAS typically uses RAID 1, which halves usable storage. The ASUSTOR AS5402T is a 2-bay with four NVMe slots for buyers who prioritize SSD speed; choose the UGREEN DH4300 Plus for four hard-drive bays.
 Do any NAS units under $500 support 10GbE? Neither pick includes 10GbE or a PCIe slot for adding it. The ASUSTOR provides dual 2.5GbE, and the UGREEN provides one 2.5GbE port.

 I have run a NAS in my house for the better part of a decade, and in that time the box in the closet has quietly become the most important piece of hardware I own. It holds every photo my family has taken, every document I would cry to lose, the Plex library that keeps the TV happy, and a growing pile of self-hosted apps that replaced a dozen cloud subscriptions. So when someone asks me which NAS to buy on a budget in 2026, I do not treat it as a small question. This is the machine your digital life sits on, and the market shifted hard this year in a way that changes the old easy answer.
 The short version is this. The reflexive advice for years was just buy a Synology, and for Plex in particular that advice is now wrong. Synology gutted hardware transcoding on its newest models and tightened its drive compatibility, so the brand that used to be the safe default is the one I now steer media-focused buyers away from. In its place, UGREEN and TerraMaster came in with Intel chips, real Quick Sync transcoding, faster networking, and open enough software that you can run their OS or wipe it for TrueNAS. These are the five budget NAS options I would actually put my own money on today, and just as importantly, which one fits which kind of person.
 What actually matters in a budget NAS in 2026
 Before the picks, let me tell you what I look at, because spec sheets are noisy and most of the numbers do not matter. Three things decide whether a budget NAS is good, and everything else is detail.
 The first is the CPU, specifically whether it has Intel Quick Sync. If you plan to run Plex or Jellyfin and stream to phones, tablets, or an older TV, your NAS will need to transcode, which means re-encoding video on the fly into a format the client can play. Quick Sync is Intel’s hardware engine that does this cheaply and quietly, and a small Intel chip with Quick Sync will out-transcode a much beefier CPU that lacks it. This single feature is why the recommendations moved this year. An ARM-based NAS or a crippled-GPU Synology will choke on the exact job most people buy a NAS to do.
 The second is drives and bays. A NAS is storage first, and how many drives it holds decides how much you can store and how safe that storage is. Two bays gives you a mirror, which survives one dead disk. Four bays gives you room to grow and better redundancy math. I nudge most people to four bays even if they start with two drives, because expanding later is painful and drives are the cheapest part of the whole equation over the life of the box.
 The third is the software and how locked down it is. A prebuilt NAS lives or dies on its operating system and app store. Synology’s DSM is still the nicest software in the category, which is the whole reason people put up with the hardware regressions. UGREEN and TerraMaster ship younger software that is improving fast, and crucially they let you wipe it and install TrueNAS or Unraid if you would rather own the stack. That escape hatch matters, because it means the hardware is never wasted even if you outgrow the vendor’s OS.
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: the best all-around pick
 This is the one I hand people who ask for a single answer. The UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus is a four-bay NAS built around an Intel Pentium Gold with Quick Sync, so it handles real 4K HDR transcodes that Synology’s current lineup cannot touch. It takes up to 64GB of DDR5, has two M.2 NVMe slots for a fast cache or all-flash pool, and it is the only NAS on this list with built-in 10GbE alongside a 2.5GbE port. That combination of transcoding muscle, memory headroom, and networking is genuinely rare at this price.
 What sells me is the flexibility. UGREEN’s own NASync software has matured into a clean, Synology-style experience with an app store, photo sync, and backup tools, so you can treat it as a turnkey appliance out of the box. But because it exposes standard hardware, you can also wipe it and run TrueNAS Scale or even Unraid, turning it into a proper virtualization and storage host. You are not locked in, which is exactly what I want from a box I plan to keep for five years. Check current price before buying: it is not the cheapest thing here, but it is the one I would least likely regret, and it is the machine that pairs perfectly with a compute-focused mini PC Proxmox node .
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800: the best cheap Plex box
 The UGREEN NASync DXP2800 is the value play, and it is the model I see recommended over and over in the self-hosting communities right now. Check its current price before deciding what to spend on your first server. It is a two-bay unit on an Intel N100, which is the same efficient little chip powering half the good budget mini PCs on the market, and critically it includes Quick Sync. That means a NAS that transcodes Plex properly, sips power, and stays quiet enough to live on a shelf in a living room.
 You give up bays and expansion compared to the DXP4800 Plus. Two drives means a mirror and not much room to grow, and there is a single M.2 slot rather than two. But for a household that wants a Plex server, phone photo backups, and a handful of self-hosted apps, this is plenty, and the N100 has enough headroom to run a few Docker containers without complaint. This is the NAS I recommend to friends who are nervous about the hobby and do not want to overspend before they know they will stick with it. It does the core job well and leaves the door open to upgrade later.
 TerraMaster F4-424 Pro: the best base for TrueNAS or Proxmox
 If you already know you want to run TrueNAS, Unraid, or Proxmox and treat the vendor OS as disposable, the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro is the smart buy. It packs an Intel Core i3 N305, an eight-core chip that is a real step up from the N100 in both raw compute and transcoding headroom, into a four-bay chassis with dual M.2 slots and support for 32GB of DDR5. On paper it undercuts the UGREEN four-bay while giving you nearly as much hardware.
 The reason I frame it as a TrueNAS base rather than a general recommendation is TerraMaster’s own software, TOS, which is functional but the weakest of the prebuilt operating systems here. The good news is that the F4-424 Pro exposes a standard UEFI BIOS, so you can plug in a USB stick and install TrueNAS Scale or Proxmox VE cleanly, and that is exactly how most enthusiasts run it. Do that and you get a powerful, open four-bay box that will happily host a ZFS pool, a stack of containers, and a couple of VMs; check current price before buying. If you want a turnkey appliance experience, buy UGREEN. If you want a strong x86 foundation to build your own stack on, this is the value leader.
 Synology DS224+: still fine, but know what you are buying
 I cannot write this list without addressing Synology directly, because it is still what most people type into a search box first. The Synology DS224+ is a competent two-bay NAS with an Intel Celeron J4125 that does include Quick Sync, and its DSM software remains the best in the business for backups, Time Machine targets, and the excellent Synology Photos app. If your priority is a rock-solid, low-fuss backup and file-sync appliance for the family, it earns its place and I still recommend it in that role.
 But be clear-eyed about why it is on this list and where it sits. This is an older-generation model, and the reason I point media buyers at UGREEN instead is the direction Synology has taken its newer units, stripping usable transcoding and locking down drive compatibility. The DS224+ still transcodes because it predates that shift, but it is a two-bay box with limited memory and a CPU that will feel its age on heavy 4K libraries. Buy it for what DSM does beautifully, which is quietly protecting your data. Do not buy it expecting it to be the transcoding monster the UGREEN and TerraMaster boxes are, and do not assume the newer Synology models are a safe upgrade, because for Plex they are a step backward.
 The DIY TrueNAS build: the best value per terabyte
 For the person who cares most about maximum storage for the least money and enjoys the tinkering, nothing prebuilt beats rolling your own. A DIY TrueNAS build can start with an Intel N100 mini PC or a small ITX board, a few sticks of RAM, and either a drive cage or a cheap HBA card to add SATA ports. Put TrueNAS Scale on it and you get ZFS, the same enterprise-grade filesystem the expensive units run, with snapshots, checksums, and self-healing, and you get it with zero license fees and zero app lock-in.
 The honest trade is time and support. You are the one choosing parts, flashing an HBA, and reading forum threads when a pool will not import. There is more upfront friction than plugging in a UGREEN and clicking through a wizard. But the payoff is real. Dollar for dollar and terabyte for terabyte, a DIY box wins, especially once you get to six or eight drives where prebuilt units get expensive fast. This is also the build I point people to when they want ECC memory for maximum data integrity, since most prebuilt budget units do not offer it. If you already have a spare mini PC lying around, the marginal cost to turn it into a capable NAS is small, and it is a fantastic way to learn how storage actually works before you spend real money.
 How to pick between them
 Cut through all of it with a few questions. If you want one box that does everything well and you do not want to think hard, buy the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus. If you want the cheapest thing that still transcodes Plex properly, buy the UGREEN DXP2800. If you are set on TrueNAS or Proxmox and want the strongest x86 base for the money, buy the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro. If your job is backups and file sync for the family and you love polished software, the Synology DS224+ is still a fine appliance. And if you want the most storage per dollar and enjoy the build, roll a DIY TrueNAS box.
 Whatever you choose, remember two things I learned the expensive way. First, a NAS with no backup is not a backup, so plan for a second copy of anything irreplaceable, whether that is a cloud sync or an external drive you rotate. Second, protect the box from power problems with a proper UPS for your NAS , because a hard shutdown mid-write is one of the few things that can genuinely corrupt a storage pool. The NAS is the foundation, and it is worth building on carefully.
 The Bottom Line
 The story of NAS buying in 2026 is that the safe default changed. For years the answer was Synology, and this year that answer broke for anyone who cares about Plex, because Synology stripped the transcoding and tightened the drive locks that made its boxes worth the premium. UGREEN and TerraMaster stepped straight into that gap with Intel chips, real Quick Sync, faster networking, and software open enough to run their OS or your own. If I had to spend my own money today on one budget NAS to anchor a self-hosting setup, it would be the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus, with the DXP2800 as the value pick and a DIY TrueNAS box for anyone who wants to build. Buy the one that matches how you actually work, put a backup and a UPS behind it, and it will quietly run your digital life for years.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best budget NAS for Plex in 2026? + For most people it is the UGREEN NASync DXP2800 if you want cheap and simple, or the DXP4800 Plus if you want room to grow. Both use Intel chips with Quick Sync, which is what actually matters for Plex, because Quick Sync is the hardware transcoding engine that lets one small box turn a 4K file into a stream your phone or old TV can play without melting the CPU. The important 2026 twist is that Synology quietly crippled transcoding on its newest models, so the old default answer of just buy a Synology no longer holds if media is your main job. If you only care about backups and file sync, a Synology DS224+ is still fine, but for Plex I steer people to UGREEN or TerraMaster now.
 Why should I avoid the newest Synology models for Plex? + Because Synology removed or disabled the hardware transcoding that made them the classic Plex pick. The 2025 and 2026 generation either ships with no usable GPU or has Quick Sync switched off in software, so a file that needs transcoding leans entirely on a weak CPU and stutters. Synology also started restricting which drives you can use in newer units, which pushes you toward their branded disks at a markup. Their DSM software is still excellent for backups, Time Machine, and photo sync, so I do not tell people to throw out a Synology they own. I just stop recommending the current lineup for anyone whose top priority is transcoding media.
 Should I buy a prebuilt NAS or build my own with TrueNAS? + Buy prebuilt if you want it working the same evening and you value support, a clean app store, and a small quiet box. Build your own if you want the most storage per dollar, full control of ZFS, and no software lock-in, and you are comfortable spending an afternoon in a BIOS and a config screen. A DIY TrueNAS box on an Intel N100 mini PC plus a drive cage often beats a prebuilt on raw value, especially at higher drive counts. The catch is that you are your own support desk. For a first NAS where you are still learning, I usually suggest a prebuilt UGREEN or TerraMaster, then build a DIY box later once you know what you actually use.
 How many drive bays do I need for a home NAS? + Two bays is the honest floor and it covers a lot of homes, giving you one drive of redundancy in a mirror so a single disk failure does not lose data. But two bays fills up fast once you add a Plex library, phone backups, and a few VMs, and expanding a two bay unit usually means replacing both disks. Four bays is the sweet spot I point most self-hosters to, because it lets you start with two drives and grow, and it supports better redundancy layouts. Go past four only if you are hoarding large media libraries or running many services. Remember that a NAS is for storage, and compute heavy work is often better on a separate mini PC.
 Do I need 10GbE networking on my NAS? + Most people do not, at least not yet. A single spinning hard drive tops out well under what 2.5GbE already delivers, so 2.5GbE is the right default for a 2026 home NAS and it is now cheap and common. You start to want 10GbE when you run an all flash NAS, edit large video files straight off the box, or move huge datasets between machines regularly. The nice thing about a unit like the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is that it includes 10GbE, so you can start on 2.5GbE and light up the faster port later when the rest of your network catches up. Match the NAS to your switch, not to a spec sheet you will not use for two years.

 Why Hardware Transcoding Matters for Plex
 Transcoding converts video from one format/quality to another. When a client device can't play your original file (wrong codec, slow internet, bandwidth limits), Plex transcodes it on the fly.
 Software vs Hardware Transcoding
 Software transcoding: Uses CPU to convert video. Very CPU-intensive. A 4K HEVC transcode can max out most NAS processors.
 Hardware transcoding: Uses dedicated GPU/encoder (Intel Quick Sync). 10x more efficient. Same NAS can handle 4-6 transcodes simultaneously.
 Intel Quick Sync is Intel's integrated GPU technology. It handles video encoding/decoding with minimal CPU usage. This is why Intel-based Synology models dramatically outperform AMD models for Plex - despite AMD having faster raw CPU performance.
 When You Need Transcoding
 Remote streaming: Plex automatically transcodes to match available bandwidth
 Incompatible clients: Some devices can't play HEVC/H.265, requiring transcoding to H.264
 Subtitles: Image-based subtitles (PGS, VOBSUB) require "burning in" via transcode
 4K → 1080p: When clients or bandwidth can't handle 4K
 Bandwidth limits: User-set quality limits trigger transcoding
 When You DON'T Need Transcoding
 If all these conditions are met, you can skip transcoding entirely (Direct Play):
 All clients support your video codecs (H.264/HEVC)
 You only stream locally (no remote access)
 You use text-based subtitles (SRT, ASS) only
 Your files match client capabilities
 If you only do Direct Play, AMD models like the DS923+ work fine for Plex. But most users need transcoding at least occasionally - and that's where Intel wins.

 Can the Synology DS923+ run Plex?
 Yes, but with limitations. The DS923+ uses an AMD Ryzen processor without Intel Quick Sync, so it can only do software transcoding. This limits it to 1-2 simultaneous transcodes with high CPU usage. It works fine for Direct Play (no transcoding) but isn't recommended if you need regular transcoding.
 Do I need Plex Pass for hardware transcoding?
 Yes. Hardware transcoding is a Plex Pass exclusive feature. Without Plex Pass ($5/month or $120 lifetime), Plex uses software transcoding only - even on Intel-based NAS models. Plex Pass also enables HDR tone mapping and other premium features.
 How many streams can a Synology DS224+ handle?
 The DS224+ can handle 2-4 simultaneous 1080p hardware transcodes, or 1-2 4K to 1080p transcodes. For Direct Play streams (no transcoding), it can handle 10+ simultaneous streams limited only by network bandwidth. Actual performance depends on source files and client capabilities.
 Is 2GB RAM enough for Plex on Synology?
 2GB works for basic Plex use with small libraries (<5,000 items). For larger libraries, running Docker alongside Plex, or heavy use, upgrade to 6GB (the maximum for DS224+/DS423+). More RAM improves library browsing speed and thumbnail loading.
 Can Synology transcode 4K HDR content?
 Intel-based Synology models (DS224+, DS423+) can transcode 4K HDR with tone mapping, converting HDR to SDR for non-HDR displays. This requires Plex Pass. AMD models cannot do this efficiently. For best results, use devices that support Direct Play of 4K HDR.
 What's better for Plex: Synology or QNAP?
 Both work well with the right hardware. For transcoding, choose Intel-based models from either brand. Synology offers better software (DSM) and easier setup. QNAP offers more hardware options and often better value. The Synology DS224+ and QNAP TS-264 are comparable choices for Plex.
 Final Verdict: Best Synology NAS for Plex
 For most users: Synology DS224+ (~$300) 
 The DS224+ offers the best combination of price, performance, and transcoding capability. Its Intel J4125 processor handles hardware transcoding beautifully, supporting 2-4 simultaneous 1080p streams or 4K HDR tone mapping. At $300, it's an incredible value for a dedicated Plex server.
 For large libraries: Synology DS423+ (~$470) 
 If you need more than 44TB of storage or want RAID 5 redundancy, the DS423+ offers four bays with identical transcoding performance. The extra $170 buys you room to grow.
 Avoid for Plex: DS923+, DS723+, DS1522+ 
 These AMD-based models are excellent NAS units for file storage, Docker, and business use - but their lack of Intel Quick Sync makes them poor choices for Plex transcoding. Only choose these if you exclusively do Direct Play.

7 Best NAS Drives for Home Media Servers 2026 
 7 Best NAS Drives for Home Media Servers 2026

 The 7 best NAS drives for home media servers in 2026, ranked by Plex transcoding performance and overall value. 
 You want to run Plex at home without buffering, stuttering, or transcoding failures. The wrong NAS turns movie night into a loading screen. The right one handles multiple 4K streams while you barely notice it’s there.
 The key spec for Plex is hardware transcoding. You need an Intel or AMD CPU with Quick Sync or equivalent hardware acceleration. ARM-based NAS units cannot transcode on the fly, which means any device that doesn’t direct play your files will stutter or fail entirely. Every NAS on this list supports hardware-accelerated Plex transcoding.
 The best NAS drives for home media servers in 2026 are:
 Synology DS224+ — best overall for most Plex users
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus — best for 4K transcoding power
 Synology DS923+ — best for large media libraries
 QNAP TS-464 — best Synology alternative with HDMI
 ASUSTOR AS5402T — best for speed enthusiasts
 TerraMaster F4-423 — best budget 4-bay
 TerraMaster F2-223 — best budget entry point
 Quick Picks

 Synology DS224+ Most Plex users 2 Intel Celeron J4125 2 GB ~$300 DSM software + Quick Sync 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus 4K power users 4 Intel Pentium Gold 8505 8 GB ~$450 10GbE + 4K multi-stream 
 Synology DS923+ Large libraries 4 (exp. to 9) AMD Ryzen R1600 4 GB ~$550 Expandable to 9 bays via DX517 
 QNAP TS-464 HDMI direct output 4 Intel Celeron N5105 8 GB ~$500 HDMI 2.0 for direct TV output 
 ASUSTOR AS5402T Speed enthusiasts 2 Intel Celeron N5105 4 GB ~$350 2.5GbE + M.2 NVMe SSD caching

 TerraMaster F2-223 Budget entry 2 Intel Celeron N4505 4 GB ~$180 Cheapest Intel NAS for Plex 
 Table of Contents
 1. Synology DS224+ 
 Best for: Most home Plex users who want reliable transcoding and the best NAS software.
 The Synology DS224+ remains the default recommendation for home Plex servers in 2026, and for good reason. The Intel Celeron J4125 CPU handles Quick Sync hardware transcoding, which means one to two simultaneous 4K-to-1080p streams without breaking a sweat. For a household where two or three people might be streaming different content at the same time, that’s plenty.
 What makes the DS224+ the top pick is DSM (DiskStation Manager), Synology’s operating system. It’s the most polished NAS OS available. Package Center lets you install Plex with two clicks. The mobile app handles file management remotely. Hyper Backup automates offsite copies of your media library to cloud storage. The learning curve is shallow enough that someone who has never owned a NAS can have Plex running within an hour of unboxing.
 The 2 GB of RAM is the weak spot. It handles Plex fine, but if you plan to run Docker containers alongside Plex (Sonarr, Radarr, or other automation tools), upgrade to 6 GB or 18 GB. Synology charges a premium for official RAM, but third-party modules work and cost half as much.
 One thing I should mention: the DS224+ does not support NVMe SSD caching. If you need SSD read/write caching for faster library browsing, look at the ASUSTOR AS5402T or step up to the DS923+.
 Pros: Best-in-class DSM software, reliable Intel Quick Sync transcoding, huge community and plugin ecosystem, very quiet operation.
 Cons: Only 2 GB RAM stock (upgradable), no NVMe SSD caching, 2-bay limits total storage to ~44 TB with current drives.
 Pricing: ~$300 diskless at synology.com 
 2. UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 
 Best for: Users who need serious 4K transcoding power at a mid-range price.
 UGREEN entered the NAS market in 2024, and the DXP4800 Plus is the model that made people pay attention. The Intel Pentium Gold 8505 processor is substantially more powerful than the Celeron chips in most consumer NAS devices. In real-world testing, it handles three simultaneous 4K-to-1080p transcodes without CPU usage exceeding 40%. That’s headroom most sub-$500 NAS devices can’t match.
 The hardware spec sheet reads like a NAS costing twice the price: 8 GB RAM (expandable to 64 GB), four drive bays for up to 136 TB of raw storage, a 10GbE port for local network transfers, and two M.2 NVMe slots for SSD caching. If you’re editing video files on your NAS or transferring large media libraries, that 10GbE connection changes the experience entirely.
 The catch is software maturity. UGOS (UGREEN’s NAS operating system) is functional but young. It supports Docker, Plex, and basic file services, but it lacks the depth of Synology’s DSM or QNAP’s QTS. App selection is limited compared to Synology’s Package Center. Community support is growing but thin.
 Honestly, if you’re comfortable with Docker and don’t need a hand-holding app store, the hardware value here is hard to beat. If you want a polished plug-and-play experience, stick with Synology.
 Pros: Intel Pentium Gold 8505 crushes Plex transcoding, 10GbE networking, 8 GB RAM expandable to 64 GB, strong price-to-performance ratio.
 Cons: Software is still maturing (UGOS is version 1.x), smaller app ecosystem than Synology or QNAP, limited community resources for troubleshooting.
 Pricing: ~$450 diskless at nas.ugreen.com 
 3. Synology DS923+ 
 Best for: Users with large media libraries who need room to grow.
 The DS923+ is the NAS you buy when you know your library will keep growing. It ships as a 4-bay unit, but connect a Synology DX517 expansion unit and you have 9 bays total. At 22 TB per drive, that’s nearly 200 TB of raw storage before RAID overhead. For a media collector who measures their library in tens of terabytes, that expansion path matters.
 The AMD Ryzen R1600 dual-core processor handles Plex adequately for direct play and light transcoding, but it lacks Intel Quick Sync. For hardware-accelerated transcoding, you’ll need a Plex Pass and the right container configuration. Alternatively, Synology sells the E10M20-T1 10GbE/M.2 combo adapter, which adds NVMe caching and faster networking in one expansion card.
 Backing up a step: if your Plex clients all direct play (Apple TV 4K, NVIDIA Shield, most smart TVs with modern apps), the lack of Quick Sync is irrelevant. Direct play sends the file as-is with zero transcoding. The DS923+ handles dozens of simultaneous direct play streams without effort.
 The premium price reflects Synology’s build quality, DSM software, and long-term update support. Synology NAS devices from 2018 still receive DSM updates.
 Pros: Expandable to 9 bays via DX517, excellent DSM software, ECC RAM support, 10GbE upgradeable, long-term software updates.
 Cons: No Intel Quick Sync (AMD Ryzen R1600), $550 before drives, expansion unit sold separately (~$500).
 Pricing: ~$550 diskless at newegg.com 
 4. QNAP TS-464 
 Best for: Users who want HDMI output and a Synology alternative.
 The QNAP TS-464 is the strongest alternative to Synology for Plex users. The Intel Celeron N5105 quad-core processor supports Quick Sync hardware transcoding, which puts it on par with the Synology DS224+ for Plex performance but in a 4-bay chassis.
 The standout feature: HDMI 2.0 output. Plug the TS-464 directly into your TV and use QNAP’s HD Station or the Plex HTPC app to browse and play media without a separate streaming device. No Apple TV needed. No Chromecast. Just a NAS connected to a TV. For a dedicated media room setup, this simplifies the hardware chain.
 QNAP’s QTS operating system is powerful but less intuitive than Synology’s DSM. It exposes more configuration options, which power users appreciate but newcomers find overwhelming. The mobile app is decent. Docker support through Container Station works well for running Sonarr, Radarr, and other Plex automation tools.
 Quick reality check: QNAP has had more security vulnerabilities than Synology in recent years. Keep QTS updated, disable UPnP, and don’t expose the admin interface to the internet. Behind a firewall with automatic updates enabled, the TS-464 is a solid daily driver.
 Pros: HDMI 2.0 output for direct TV connection, Intel Quick Sync transcoding, 8 GB RAM, two M.2 NVMe slots, 4-bay capacity.
 Cons: QTS less polished than DSM, higher security vulnerability history than Synology, power consumption higher than competitors.
 Pricing: ~$500 diskless at qnap.com 
 5. ASUSTOR AS5402T 
 Best for: Enthusiasts who want fast local transfers and SSD caching on a 2-bay NAS.
 The AS5402T packs enthusiast-grade networking into a 2-bay form factor. Dual 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet ports (with link aggregation) and two M.2 NVMe SSD slots for caching. For a household where the NAS feeds media to multiple rooms over a wired network, that 2.5GbE speed makes library browsing and thumbnail loading noticeably snappier than standard gigabit.
 The Intel Celeron N5105 CPU handles Plex transcoding through Intel Quick Sync, matching the QNAP TS-464 and TerraMaster F4-423 on raw transcoding capability. 4 GB of RAM (expandable to 16 GB) is adequate for Plex with a few Docker containers running alongside.
 ASUSTOR’s ADM (ASUSTOR Data Master) operating system sits between QNAP and Synology in terms of polish. It’s cleaner than QTS but not as refined as DSM. The App Central store includes Plex, Portainer, and most common NAS applications. ASUSTOR has a smaller community than Synology, so troubleshooting niche issues requires more self-reliance.
 At $350 diskless, the AS5402T offers the best networking specs of any 2-bay NAS on this list. If 2.5GbE or SSD caching matters to your setup, this is the pick.
 Pros: Dual 2.5GbE with link aggregation, M.2 NVMe SSD caching, Intel Quick Sync transcoding, competitive pricing for the specs.
 Cons: Smaller community than Synology, ADM software less polished, 2-bay limits total storage capacity.
 Pricing: ~$350 diskless at asustor.com 
 6. TerraMaster F4-423 
 Best for: Budget-conscious buyers who need 4-bay capacity with Plex transcoding.
 The F4-423 is the cheapest 4-bay NAS on this list that can actually handle Plex hardware transcoding. The Intel Celeron N5105 CPU matches the QNAP TS-464 and ASUSTOR AS5402T on processing power, and the 4 GB of RAM is sufficient for Plex with light container workloads.

 How We Chose These
 We filtered the NAS market for one requirement above all others: the CPU must support hardware-accelerated Plex transcoding. ARM-based NAS units were excluded entirely because they cannot transcode media on the fly, which breaks the Plex experience for any client that doesn’t support direct play.
 From the remaining Intel and AMD-powered options, we ranked by Plex transcoding headroom (how many simultaneous streams the CPU handles), storage expandability, network speed, software maturity, and price. We weighted real-world Plex benchmarks over synthetic CPU scores, since transcoding performance depends heavily on Quick Sync support and driver optimization.
 We also factored in community support and long-term software updates. A NAS is a 5-to-10-year purchase. Brands that ship regular security patches and OS updates scored higher than those with spotty track records.
 The Bottom Line

 If you need 4K transcoding power that outclasses everything in this price range, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus at ~$450 delivers hardware that punches well above its weight.  Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best NAS drive for home media servers?
 The Synology DS224+ is the best NAS for home media servers in 2026. It combines Intel Quick Sync hardware transcoding for Plex, the industry-leading DSM operating system, and a $300 price point that makes it accessible to most home users. It handles one to two simultaneous 4K-to-1080p transcodes without strain.
 Is the Synology DS224+ better than the QNAP TS-464 for Plex?
 The DS224+ has better software (DSM vs QTS) and is $200 cheaper. The TS-464 has more drive bays (4 vs 2), HDMI output for direct TV connection, and 8 GB of RAM vs 2 GB. Pick the DS224+ for simplicity and value. Pick the TS-464 if you need 4 bays or want to plug the NAS directly into a TV without a streaming device.
 Can an ARM-based NAS run Plex?
 ARM-based NAS units can run the Plex server software, but they cannot hardware-transcode video. If every client on your network supports direct play (Apple TV 4K, NVIDIA Shield, most modern smart TVs), an ARM NAS works fine. If any client needs transcoding (web browsers, older Roku devices, mobile over cellular), you need an Intel or AMD CPU with hardware acceleration.
 How many hard drives do I need for a Plex NAS?
 For most home users, a 2-bay NAS with one drive is enough to start. A single 16 TB drive holds roughly 3,200 movies in 1080p or 800 in 4K. Adding a second drive in RAID 1 (mirror) protects your library from a single drive failure. Users with libraries over 30 TB should consider 4-bay models for RAID 5 protection and more capacity.
 Does the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus work well with Plex?
 Yes. The Intel Pentium Gold 8505 in the DXP4800 Plus handles Plex hardware transcoding very well. In testing, it manages three simultaneous 4K-to-1080p transcodes at under 40% CPU usage. The 10GbE port also makes large file transfers significantly faster than gigabit NAS devices. The main trade-off is software maturity: UGOS is functional but less polished than Synology’s DSM.
